en: A Commentary on the "Instructions for Pure-Minded Contemplation to Elicit the Truth," Volume One (with Preface).
Composed by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Yunkan.
Now, those who study the Way take self-illumination as their foundation, while those who establish words take benefiting others as their primary principle. In the past, the Sages...
The worthy leader follows these two admonitions to observe that one thereby clarifies the teaching of benefiting oneself and others.

Although our ancestor Nanshan entrusted his instruction to compassion and forbearance, could he have had no concern for those who would come after? I, Yu, have for twenty years been fortunate enough to receive the Way of the Great Master;
the various commentaries on the scriptures I have compiled amount to nearly one hundred fascicles. Alas! To record words while forgetting the underlying principle—this is a great pity.

Is it not also a sickness for those who observe? This year I am forty-one; realizing that more than half of my life in this floating world has passed, I have adopted this contemplation as a method for governing the mind.
One day during a lecture, a disciple whose understanding was still dimmed requested that I further elaborate upon these words.
I have thus compiled them into three fascicles, titled *Fazhen* (Unfolding the Truth), wishing to enable those who tread this path to unfold their true nature and return to the source.
If this is so, then is it not the case that one stands on tiptoe before the brightness of the sun, desiring to benefit all things?
This preface was written on the day of the full moon in the third month of the year Wuyou (the fifth year of the Qingli era) at the Jingzhu Monastery lecture hall in Qiantang.
Preface to the *Dharmas of Contemplation for Purifying the Mind*, composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Yuánzhào of Yúháng Commandery.
Nothing is more immediate or easier than one’s own mind; yet, from death to birth, one remains entirely unaware of it. Its essence is luminous and translucent.

Because its capacity is all-encompassing, it causes a single delusion to suddenly give rise to all phenomena. It is like a precious mirror in which images appear due to external light, or like a long river whose waves stir because of clarity.
To claim that the mind is a separate entity and that the mind is transformed by objects is to allow the dust of sensory conditions to be drawn in and accumulated, forming knots of exhaustion.
Thus one sinks through the various realms of existence, submerging one's own spirit; in other destinies there is no awareness, and among human beings there is no discernment.
Those with little learning, even if they have heard and studied much, mostly fall into perverse delusion; they chase after fame and become attached to intellectual understanding.
There are even those who travel from south of the Yangtze to north of it in search of Bodhi, yet their views are crooked and their minds perverse, never upright.

Like wild monkeys leaping about or domestic dogs lingering about, they weary my Holy Master, who leans down to instruct them by the ear and compassionately leaves behind the wondrous medicine, precisely pointing out the root of their ailment.
Encompassing both vehicles (*yāna*) and serving as the gateway through which all practices (*caryā*) are realized, this work entrusts the direct guidance of others to manifest its vast compassion.
It charges us to peer into its depths while relying upon its revelation of the secret and sublime; it sternly rebukes mere scholastic debate and earnestly exhorts the cultivation of practice.

Thus, while the masters of antiquity transmitted the tradition by simultaneously propagating both doctrine (*śāsana*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), using various scriptural sections (*nikāya*) to open understanding through doctrine, this text instead demonstrates the path of cultivation through contemplation. Indeed, one cannot be said to lack eyes for this.

Wandering through the world is not merely counting another's treasures; one must believe that delusion arises from the True. When the manifestation of the body appears before you, realize that delusion is itself the True;
it is not obtained from another. Those who read this should understand the essential point of purifying the mind.
A Commentary on the "Instructions for Observing the Mind with Purity" (Jìngxīn Jièguān Fāzhēn Chāo), Volume One.
Composed by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Shi Yunkan.
The Dharma of Observing the Mind with Purity.
This admonition for practitioners arises precisely because many students remain stalled in the maladies of the mind and have not yet reached the source of the Dharma.
Therefore, our Great Master, moved by compassion, rescued them from these inverted attachments and opened up two paths to encompass the three capacities of beings:

first clarifying the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and finally extending the practice of the Greater Vehicle (Mahāyāna). The preceding twenty-five chapters manifest self-benefit, while the subsequent four chapters reveal [the benefit of others].
In benefiting others, there is nothing that does not encompass and synthesize the various scriptures to elucidate one’s own realization, so as to enable all who come to realize the Supreme Vehicle.

Furthermore, it ensures that those who contemplate through this work will thereafter fully comprehend the nature and characteristics, the phenomena and principles, the causes and effects, the stages and positions, and the manifest wisdoms of all existence—leaving nothing unexhausted.
Thus, even the eighty thousand dharma-gates and five thousand volumes of sutras need not be awaited.
To encompass everything through a single gateway is like entering the door of a temple and beholding the full splendor of its ancestral shrines;
is this not what is meant by the statement that "within a single character lies infinite meaning"? Furthermore, all phenomena are rooted in one's own mind;
if the mind is luminous and pure, all phenomena become clearly manifest. To be able to penetrate this principle is—
Since it is capable of encompassing everything, how could one allow knowledge and views to be hindered by the verbal elaboration or brevity of the explanations?

Therefore, the five-character titles now penetrate through all the chapters. Furthermore, as the analysis and explanation of the titles are already clearly revealed in the first section, they are omitted here in this commentary;
lecturers should extract them from the subsequent text and present them at the appropriate time.

However, regarding the coarse distinction between the object and the subject: for instance, the single character *xin* (心) belongs to the object (*so*), while the four characters *jing yu jie guan fa* (淨與誡觀法) belong to the subject (*neng*).
It is by relying on these provisional dharmas that one is able to purify the mind. As for what is called "mind" (*xin*), the Sanskrit term is *citta*, which is translated as "mind.
If discussed from the perspective of the limited, it refers merely to the purification of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). Therefore, it is said below: "defilement" (*gou*).
The gradual extinction of defilements causes the mind to become increasingly clear and pure; this refers to practices such as the contemplations of the five *sthāpanā-cittas*.
Speaking in terms of the broader scope, it means that by giving rise to pure faith, one returns from deluded thoughts to the single true mind. Therefore, the text below further states:
"By giving rise to the pure Mahāyāna faith, one proceeds toward the dwelling place of the *gotra* (spiritual lineage) of Bodhi. This constitutes the first title.
The two meanings of "purifying the mind" encompass both admonition and contemplation. "Admonition" (*śamatha*) means to alert or warn.

"Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*)—the Sanskrit term translated here as "contemplation"—has the meaning of observation. "Dharma" means a norm or rule; it signifies that which can serve as a standard or model to inspire understanding in others.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain.
Zhongnan Mountain is the name of a mountain in the state of Zhou. The *Yao yi* (Essential Meanings) of the Five Classics states: "The southern mountain of Chang'an is also named Taiyi.
Pan Yue’s *Guang zhong ji* (Record of Guanzhong) states: "This mountain is also called Zhongnan, meaning 'in the center of heaven.'"
It is situated to the south of the capital. Regarding "mountain" (*shan*), the *Guoyu* states: "A mountain is a gathering of earth. The *Shuowen* says: "A mountain is 'to declare' (*xuan*);
it declares the vital energy (*qi*) to produce all things. Today, Zhongnan is a place of profound seclusion for great masters.
As for "śramaṇa," it is a general term for those who have left the household life; the Sanskrit term *śramaṇa* is translated here as "diligent cessation" (*qinxi*).

This means that because one exerts effort to extinguish suffering and sever afflictions—or conversely, because one transforms the path of deprivation into a fertile field of merit—one is able to eliminate the famine of sentient beings by practicing the Eightfold Noble Path and thereby severing all false paths.
As it says in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Śramaṇa" means "deprivation," and "na" means "path. Such a path severs everything.
Because he has severed all paths [of affliction], for this reason he cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path as a *śramaṇa*.
Since he attains the fruits from within this path, he is called a *śramaṇa*. Therefore, the name *śramaṇa* applies to both cause and fruit.

Thus, our Great Master is a *śramaṇa* who is a superior person (*upāsaka*) based on the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*) and practices Mahāyāna contemplation, such as the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*.

How could this samādhi be practiced by those of inferior stations? (Pratyutpanna-samādhi is translated as "Buddhas Standing Before One," meaning that one is able to see the Buddhas of the present in the ten directions standing before oneself within meditative concentration.
The Great Master conducted twenty or more assemblies in total, with each session limited to three months. Thus we know that his essence was lofty while his traces were humble;
he manifested in the body of a Vinaya Master to expound the Vinaya Piṭaka. Therefore, the world addressed him as "Vinaya Master. Furthermore, the Buddha...

One who has left the household life, whose words are intimate [with truth], who realizes the mind and penetrates the source, and who understands the dharma of non-action (*asamskṛta*), is called a *śramaṇa*.
As for "Śākya," it is said in full that this translates as "Capable Benevolence" (*Nengren*). Originally, Śini Loucong was banished and dwelt among the Snow Mountains;
his virtue attracted people like a marketplace until he became a powerful state. His father, the King, sighed from afar, "My son is Capable Benevolent," and thus the clan name was changed to Śākya.
From Kāśyapa onwards, the lineage was succeeded by the Gautama clan. King Śuddhodana occupied the fifth generation, the Buddha the sixth, and the one currently being discussed occupies the seventh.
Because the fivefold assembly of renunciants takes the Buddha as their teacher, the Āgamas state:
"The four great rivers flow into the ocean and no longer retain their original names; likewise, those of the four castes who renounce the world all adopt the name of the Great Teacher, Śākya."

Regarding names and titles: in the Western Regions (India), because calling by name is considered honorable, there are instances where a son’s name incorporates those of his parents; yet in later generations, this practice was not followed.

In the Middle Kingdom (China), because avoiding the use of names is considered honorable, when one hears the names of deceased parents, the heart is struck with alarm and grief (the character *qú* [pronounced *jù*] denotes shock and sorrow);
therefore, people avoid these names. However, one does not avoid them within the ancestral temple, nor does one avoid them when composing formal texts or when discussing the Way.

"Xuān" is the name of the Great Master. Matters concerning his spiritual resonance and such are as described in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Royal Sòng Dynasty*, which the compiler also recounts;
that is to say, the compiler transmits ancient surviving writings, "recounting but not composing."
Homage. "Homage" (jing-li) means reverence and solemnity. Regarding "rites" (li), the *Zhongni yanju* states: "Rites are principle; the noble person does not move unless there is principle.
It further states: "Rites are the body (just as one has a human body); if the body is incomplete, the person is not whole."

The Master said that one who does not do this is not a complete person. If the ritual is not performed correctly, it is as if it were incomplete. According to the musical laws (*lü*), there are distinctions between large and small;
in the sequence of rites, even down to the Tathāgata and his stūpas, the fivefold assembly performs a general salutation—this too is appropriate.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of three types of salutation: first, the oral salutation (which is the lower salutation); second, the kneeling salutation where the head does not touch the ground (the middle salutation); third, the prostration where the head touches the ground.

The first [of these] belongs to the karma of speech (the term "ground" [di], which corresponds to "prostration with the head to the ground" in the *Shangli* and *Zhouli*), while the latter two belong to the karma of body.

Furthermore, when respect extends to the mind, the three karmas are complete. If one wishes to know how ritual laws differ in their orthodoxy and heterodoxy, consider the Tripitaka Master from Western India named Ratnamati;
seeing that those here below belonged to the remote frontiers and were unacquainted with ritual laws, he translated [this work].
The seven types [of prostration] are as follows: First is the prostration of the conceited mind (*māna-citta*). This refers to a lack of sincere reverence;

outwardly one appears respectful, yet inwardly arrogance and delusion increase. It is like the up-and-down motion of a pestle, or like a wooden puppet; because the human spirit is not earnest, it lacks true gravity. Second is the prostration for the sake of seeking fame (*nāma-kīrti*).

This refers to chanting with the mouth while the mind is distracted. When seeing others, the body moves with light and hurried agility; when the people have left, the body becomes sluggish and indolent.

1. Fatigue of mind (these two types of practitioners should not perform this); 2. Prostration with physical and mental reverence: when body and mind are reverent, there is no difference between form and mind;
as the Buddha previously placed his hand upon their crowns to guide and benefit humans and devas, this is the supreme merit.
Yet, although great, it does not yet give rise to wisdom, for later one often falls back; 3. Prostration that gives rise to pure wisdom: reaching the realm of the Buddha.
With the wisdom of the realms and a mind clear and sharp, one who pays homage to a single Buddha pays homage to all Buddhas;
paying homage to all Buddhas is likewise the Dharma and the Sangha of that single Buddha. Because their essence of liberation is identical, the mind becomes increasingly luminous with every thought.
With each prostration and each rising, pure karma is inexhaustible and its karmic fruition is limitless. Upon entering the Dharma-realm for the fifth time, pay homage while visualizing yourself...
The body, from its very origin, has never been separate from the *dharmadhātu*; it does not exist outside the bodies of the Buddhas, nor does it exist within them.

Its self-nature is equal, fundamentally without increase or decrease. To now pay homage to one Buddha is to pervasively reach all Buddhas, just as when a hundred thousand mirrors are suspended within a single room and a person looks into them, images appear in every mirror; the Buddha-body is pure and luminous.
They exceed mirrors in their mutual interpenetration, for there is no reflection that is not illuminated and no image that does not appear. Thus, the *Bhūmivastu-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
"Offerings made non-presence are superior to offerings made presence. Furthermore, since the virtues and functions of all Buddhas are equal, their names are likewise identical;
whichever name one invokes, there is no name that does not encompass them all. For example, if one were to invoke the name of Śākyamuni and pay homage, [the merit would be complete].
There is not a single Buddha among all Buddhas who is not fully endowed with these qualities. In the Sanskrit language, Śākyamuni means "Able One" (Néng-rén);
how could there be a single Buddha who is not an Able One? Furthermore, as for Amitāyus, how could there be a single Buddha who is not one of Long Life?

In the Sanskrit language, Maitreya means "Kindly One" (Cí-shì)—as the *Siyi jing* states, "Sentient beings who see him attain the Samādhi of the Mind of Compassion," for he gathers all beings through unconditioned compassion—how could there be...?
Are there not Buddhas other than Maitreya? Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The supreme capacity of one Buddha is equal to the supreme capacity of all Buddhas.
One who prostrates in this manner pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. This refers to practicing sincere prostration through the six correct contemplations;
it clarifies that one prostrates to the Buddha within one's own body, rather than taking the Buddha of another's body as an external object. Why is this? Because all sentient beings are Buddhas.
The nature [of all beings] is equal; yet, due solely to delusion, one pays homage exclusively to others while falsely regarding the Buddha-nature within one’s own body as evil.

If one can reflect back upon oneself, liberation will be attained. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "As one contemplates the true reality of one's own body, so too should one contemplate the Buddha.
Furthermore, cultivating clarity according to one's capacity is precisely what draws forth the Buddha-nature, until the fruit is perfected after three great eons (*trikalpāsaṃkhyeya*).
This refers to the attainment of the Buddha-nature of the fruition; how much more so for this wondrous realization, which is restricted only to the Great Sages.
As for ordinary beings of lower capacity, although they have not yet practiced it instantaneously, they cannot fail to understand it.

Just as one traveling a long road must rely on their own body, so too must one who wishes to see the Buddha-nature observe their own Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. When these are realized as identical and non-dual, this is called "right observation" and "veneration."

Seventh, regarding the equality of the true mark (*dharmatā*), the general intent is the same as before; however, whereas the previous instances involved paying homage while still maintaining the dual distinction between self and other through contemplation, this present single prostration is devoid of both self and other. Ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness, equal in essence and function.
If one perceives the Buddha as worthy of honor and reverence, one simultaneously perceives ordinary beings as base and contemptible. To give rise to such a mind constitutes a deviation.
Because it is grasped [as such], the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "This Dharma is equal, with no high or low; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because its true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is free from conceptual thought, it cannot be grasped by the mind, nor sought through signs, nor attained through ritual homage, nor discarded through arrogance.
It transcends high and low, leaves behind honor and meanness, and unifies stillness and agitation, reverence and negligence, into a single source.
To unify and perfect this single rite: when those of ordinary and shallow understanding hear of it, they may fear and instead slander it;

yet for those of superior wisdom, internal practice is equanimity while externally they accord with and cultivate respect. When the internal and external merge in harmony, this is called the "Rite of Equality.

Those who practice today, if they wish to cultivate respectful salutation, should proceed from the shallow to the profound, directing their contemplation according to their capacity, ensuring that it does not become empty.
If one treats [the Three Jewels] as empty, their merit is lost.
The Three Jewels are the treasury of *sarvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom) and the *dharmakāya*.
Although the names of the Three Jewels are one, they collectively encompass four aspects; thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "First, the essence of principle (*li-ti*)."
Regarding the three treasures: the fivefold dharma-body is the Buddha-treasure; the cessation of suffering through the principle of non-conditioned existence is the Dharma-treasure;

and the merits of the śrāvakas, both those in training and those beyond training, are the Saṃgha-treasure. Regarding the two aspects of transformation: for example, Śākyamuni, as the King of the Path, presiding over the trichiliocosm, is the Buddha-treasure;
his expounding and disseminating of the teachings of the Truths is the Dharma-treasure; and Kauṇḍinya and the other four are the Saṃgha-treasure. Thirdly, regarding the aspect of maintenance:

Statues, images, stupas, and temples constitute the Buddha Jewel; that which is transmitted on paper and silk constitutes the Dharma Jewel; and the precepts, dharmas, and ritual forms constitute the Sangha Jewel. These four are a single essence;
it is only by way of the principle of the mind-essence (*citta-tattva*) that they are distinguished into three aspects, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Thus, the Three Jewels are of the same nature: their fundamental nature is awakening, which is the Buddha-nature; their fundamental nature is quiescence, which is the Dharma-nature; and their fundamental nature is... [the Sangha-nature].
The wondrous functions of the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges correspond one-to-one with their nature, merging in such a way that there is no distinction;
this is called the "Treasury of the Sangha. In Sanskrit, it is called *kośa*, which here means "treasury" (*zàng*), taking the sense of "containing and encompassing.

This refers to the fact that the Three Jewels universally contain and receive all things without obstruction. Therefore, the opening homage of the *Awakening of Faith* states: "I take refuge in the entirety of the ten..."
The one who possesses the most supreme activity, who fully knows all forms with unimpeded mastery, and who is the Great Compassionate Savior of the World (the Buddha Jewel;
"unimpeded" means pervading the entire Dharma-realm); as well as his physical body, the Dharma-nature, the ocean of True Suchness, and the treasury of immeasurable merits (the Dharma Jewel);

and as the subsequent commentary states, "the Sangha, the treasury of boundless virtues" (the Sangha Jewel)—therefore, the meaning of "treasury" (*garbha*) mentioned here is the same as that in the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.
Regarding the term *bha*, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that *sarva* refers to all phenomena (*dharma*). Furthermore, because one has attained *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), one is called a Buddha.
Moreover, the *Sāṃkathyaviniścaya-sūtra* states that the equality of all phenomena is called *sarvajñatā*, which cannot be reached by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
It further states that because there is no obstruction regarding all phenomena, it is called *sarvajñatā*. [The term] "small" (*ksudra*) means distant.

It is said that this translation, "the Dharma-body of all-knowledge" (*sarvajña-dharmakāya*), refers on a small scale to the fivefold Dharma-body—precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—and on a large scale to the pure Dharma-body (*viśuddha-dharmakāya*). What is called "pure" refers to suchness (*tathatā*) which is free from defilement and has emerged from the entanglements;
because it is not stained by the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), "Dharma" (in this context) is that which gives rise to understanding in sentient beings as a standard of conduct.

The "body" (*kāya*) possesses three meanings: substantiality (*dravya*), basis (*āśraya*), and collection (*caya*). Furthermore, that which serves as a guide (*prati-ni*) for generating understanding in sentient beings refers to the time when one attains the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) within the path of liberation following the stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
At that time, the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) internally accords with ultimate truth (*tattva*), thus possessing the sense of being a guide and a standard of understanding.
Regarding "substantiality, basis, and collection": stainless *tathatā* (Suchness) is its substance; this is the meaning of "substance. It is like the sands of the Ganges... [and so forth].

The ten thousand virtues, along with the two bodies of retribution and transformation, constitute the basis; thus, "basis" (āśraya) has the meaning of being the support. The accumulation of permanence, bliss, self, and purity constitutes the meaning of "accumulation" (caya).
May the Sage, out of compassion, deign to hear this brief admonition for beginners according to their capacity.
These words are spoken according to my capacity, exhorted by my own intellectual power for the sake of beginners;

I do not presume to present them to those who have already attained mastery—this is merely a display of humility. I pray that you will not only bestow your virtue upon me, but also grant your protection.
If you listen with compassion and grant this request, there shall be no obstacles; if no obstacles arise, it is due to the merit of having sought such protection.
At that time, while observing the summer retreat at Xingtang Monastery in Suizhou, I composed this and sent it to Lingyan Monastery on Mount Tai to be entrusted to Cishen for preservation.
Suizhou belonged to the region of Hanyang within the Southern Route of Sui; during the Spring and Autumn period, it was part of Chu, corresponding to the territory described in the *Yugong*.
The territories of the two provinces of Jing and Liang are also mentioned in the *Zuozhuan*, which states that Dou Boibi said to the King of Chu:
"Among the states east of the Han River, Sui is the largest. Du Yu’s commentary notes: "The state of Sui is the present-day Sui County in Yiyang.
As for Xingtang, it is a specific name for a *gālan* (monastery), which is a general term; its full Sanskrit name is Saṃghārāma, which is translated here as "Garden of the Assembly."
Some say that *vihāra* means "dwelling. Regarding those who observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the section on the Retreat states:
"Because during the summer many instances of violating conduct occur, which invite both censure and grave consequences, the text says: 'From this day forward, I permit the three-month summer retreat.
Since the spring and winter periods are short, there will certainly be no disturbances; failure to conform to this communal agreement constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. However, for noble ones..."

If one applies the mind with earnestness, it must encompass both self-benefit and the benefit of others. Why is this? To receive and uphold the prohibitions and to restrain one's feet constitutes the practice of self-benefit; to establish words and teachings to instruct others constitutes the path of benefiting others. Is this not, in truth, the conduct of a Bodhisattva? Mount Tai is the easternmost of the Five Peaks. The *Bowuzhi* states that "Mount Tai is called the Son of Heaven. The *Wujing Tongyi* states: [The text continues: ...the mountain is the most majestic and the most exalted among all mountains. It is the first peak to receive the spring breath and the last to lose the autumn qi. Its height reaches the heavens, and its roots extend to the Yellow Springs. It is the gate of the world and the pivot of the four seas. Therefore, it is called the "Eastern Peak" (*Dongyue*). It is also known as the "Mountain of the Eastern Marchmount. The *Shanhaijing* says: "The Eastern Marchmount is named Mount Tai. The *Lunyu* says: "When you reach Mount Tai, you will see how great the earth is.
