This refers to the three [realms] of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, which are collectively unwholesome and thus "evil. Because there are other sūtras for each [of these], they are called "paths" (*mārga*).
These sūtras are the *Śāsanāpadeśa* (The Bequeathed Teaching). Because [such beings] greedily crave food, wealth, and sensual pleasures, they are not practitioners of the Way (*mārga-pudgala*);

because they do not conform to the square cap and square robe, they are not laypeople (*avadātavasana*). Since neither of these two positions encompasses them, they are said to be "without a name. As Aśvaghoṣa said:
Because they do not enter into either the supramundane or the mundane, and because they are not established as such, they pursue great gain;
thus, they are exclusively devoted to lip-service, flowery rhetoric, and ornate frivolous discourse, engaging in disputes and litigation, while mutually slandering and envying one another.

Their three poisons become increasingly fierce, their afflictions grow, and they sink into the ocean of suffering. Knowing [the truth] yet intentionally transgressing it, there will be no time for their liberation.

If one fails to see or hear of the appearance of a thousand Buddhas in the world due to such causes and conditions, one will exhaust the retribution of hell only to receive the body of an evil dragon.

This is the evil fruit obtained through stealing the robes and food of the Buddha, violating the precepts, and the defilement of anger, as explained in the *Andha-nāga-sūtra*. Thus one should understand the meaning:
though one knows, one cannot escape the suffering of one's karma.

*Khin* (吻) refers to the mouth; the *Shiming* (釋名) states that *khin* means *kai* (揩), which signifies wiping. *Zhuang* (莊) refers to adornment (*zhuāngyán* 莊嚴) and the patching together of elegant and ornate phrasing.
Regarding *prapañca* (戲論), the *Yinyi Zhiguī* (音義指歸) states it means "theatrical play" (*xìjù* 戲劇);
it refers to discourse characterized by frivolous, reckless, mocking, and humorous speech. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (成論) states: "Whether as one or as different..."
The treatise is titled *Xilun* (Discourse on Idle Talk). To slander with malice and jealousy is called "slander" (*bàng*); to harm the worthy is called "jealousy" (*jí*).

Regarding the "thousand Buddhas," according to the *Shijia pu* (Lineage of Śākyamuni), it states that in the Mahāyāna sūtras, there are one thousand Buddhas in each of the three periods of the three kalpas:
the past *Zhuāngyán* Kalpa, the present *Xián* Kalpa, and the future *Xīngxiù* Kalpa. Because three thousand princes attained Buddhahood in succession, they are thus called [the thousand Buddhas].
The Thousand Buddhas; the present Śākyamuni is the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa.
The evil dragon’s body is the residual retribution of hell. It was caused by the theft of a finger-ring.
As stated in the "Dragon Chapter" of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*: "There was a blind dragon named Parākrama who raised his voice and wept bitterly, acting as follows..."
"O Great Sage, World-Honored One, I pray that you will rescue and deliver me! Within my current body I am undergoing great suffering and affliction;
day and night I am constantly being bitten and eaten by various kinds of insects, dwelling in hot water without a moment's respite of joy.
The Buddha said, "Liśa, in a past life within the Buddha-dharma, you were once a bhikṣu who violated the prohibitions."

Externally manifesting signs of virtue while internally harboring greed for vast retinues and fame that spreads to the four quarters, and even receiving offerings alone and enjoying them exclusively—through such causes and conditions of evil karma, one receives this retribution of blindness. Thus one knows that the meaning of the lower [teachings] is resolved:
there is no action, yet the fruit of karma does not perish.
You should follow these admonitions and practice as described; according to the specific remedy for each ailment, there is liberation through analysis.
One cannot attain purity from the three poisons and five fetters merely by words.

Regarding the phrase "the practitioner should act according to the Dharma Master," "act" (xing) is pronounced with the second tone (as in *xià*) and means "to perform" or "to cultivate. It refers to the actual execution and cultivation of the practice known as giving (*dāna*).
The *Koukō-yen Daishō* states: "In the Buddha-dharma, what is valued is practicing according to the teaching, not the abundance of reading and recitation.
It further states: "One does not attain purity through mere verbal expression; rather, it is the one who practices according to the teaching who [attains it].

Regarding the phrase "the five fetters" (*go-ke*), it is commonly said that there are nine fetters (*ku-ke*). I suspect the character "five" (*go*) may be an error for "craving" (*ai*), "anger" (*fun*), "pride" (*man*), and "ignorance" (*mu-myō*).
Avarice, envy, doubt, and the grasping at views.

Which of these is most predominant? First treat that which is heaviest; once the heavy is lightened, the others will naturally be corrected. Don the armor of precepts and meditative concentration to crush the demonic thieves within the mind.
All causes and effects of suffering have wealth and sensual form as their root; all causes and effects of happiness have the precepts and meditative concentration as their root. Thus it is.
Since cause and effect are entirely contained within the minute dust-particles of the sentient beings' minds, why not restrain other transgressions? First, wealth and beauty are cautioned against;
first, the most serious [afflictions] are treated, which do not exceed greed, anger, and delusion. Furthermore, these three poisons arise from views and craving; thus, Master Zhiyi said:
"If one discusses the root of afflictions, they do not go beyond views and craving; as for their branches and twigs, they consist of conceptual discrimination."

The categories [of afflictions] are extremely numerous—namely the three poisons, the five hindrances, the ten fetters, the ninety-eight afflictions, the eighty-four thousand [afflictions], and even those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Now, if one can eliminate the root, then the branches and leaves will also vanish.

While the preceding lines have distinguished the "armor" [of practice] by encompassing precepts and concentration to subdue the mind, the following should now encompass wisdom; for it is through wisdom that [the root is severed].

Because it can slay the thieves, the "demon of the mind" refers precisely to the afflictions (*kleśa-māra*) that arise from the mind. Regarding the phrase "within the minute particles of the mind," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Within the minute particles of the minds of all sentient beings, there exist teacherless wisdom, unimpeded wisdom, vast wisdom, and so forth.
Thus, both good and evil causes and effects are entirely contained within the minute particles of the mind. (The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*...)
It is said that all phenomena arise solely as manifestations of the mind; all causes and effects, worlds, and even atoms derive their substance from the mind.

Furthermore, the *Qingliang* (Cool Grove) Commentary states: "To encompass all myriad existences is precisely the One Mind. The mention of "atoms" (*paramāṇu*) here serves to include the great by citing the small.
Thus, the *Huayan fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka) says: "Just as a single atom, its form is not large."
Yet it is able to contain and encompass the boundless dharma-realm;

since the dharmas as numerous as the atoms of all lands do not depart from the dharma-realm, they all appear together within a single atom. Since all dharmas do not depart from a single atom, cause and effect likewise do not depart from a single mind.
A Mahāyāna sūtra states that the eighty-four thousand karmic obstacles to the Path all have wealth and sensual desire as their root. Why is this?

Since beginningless time, sentient beings throughout the ten directions have killed one another for the sake of wealth more times than there are motes of dust, and those who have killed for the sake of sensual desire exceed even that number.
Among both the monastic and lay communities, these instances of killing for the sake of wealth and sensual desire exist even now.
Having endured millions of kinds of suffering within the one hundred and twenty-six great hells for immeasurable kalpas, they finally enter the realms of animals and hungry ghosts;
whether layperson or cleric, both are harmed by wealth and sensual desire. Rare indeed are those who can escape, having first observed the precepts and later transgressed them.
The eight lower [categories] refer to the eighty-four thousand karmas arising from the afflictions (*kleśa*). The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The Buddha taught that there are eighty thousand dharmas as medicinal remedies for the afflictions. Regarding "beginningless," this is a remote inference of past births and deaths as being infinite;
since beginningless delusion, one has never attained awakening, hence it is called "beginningless. As for "hell" (*naraka*), in Sanskrit it is called...
Among the three miserable realms (*durgati*), the *naraka* (hell) is the path of fire.
Because it is located at the very lowest part of this world-system, the treatises of the Hīnayāna state that there are eight great hells. Each hell has four gates, totaling sixteen minor hells;
these eight hells together comprise one hundred and twenty-eight, which, when combined with the original eight, total one hundred and thirty-six.
The six characters comprise twenty-six syllables; errors regarding their internal forms, widths, and quantities are as clarified in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are the Light-Bound Hells (*laghu-bandhana-naraka*), or [rebirth] among humans, or in deep mountains and vast wildernesses, or by the seashore and between the Cakravāḍa Mountains.
The *Linggan-tan* (Account of Spiritual Resonance) states: "In the profound darkness, where even the light of the sun and moon does not reach..."
Regarding that which cannot be illuminated, it further cites a verse from a sutra: "Between the two Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), one does not behold the light of the sun or moon;
hungry ghosts dwell therein to repay their past karmic debts. Or, they may be in the midst of empty space;

here, because they are currently confronted by other minor fetters, both are referred to as "great. The two groups, the "robed" and the "white-robed," refer respectively to bhikṣus and laypeople (*avadātavasana*). Although [this] is compared...
Question: Those who have fully received the precepts and laypeople who observe the five or eight precepts all maintain them at first with vigor, yet later they violate them due to laxity.
What is the appearance of the color of the monastic robes? Answer: It is purple and a light black;

it is not a primary color. The *Rites of Zhou* states: "Three dyes produce vermilion (*xūn*); five dyes produce *zēi* (*zī hóu*); seven [dyes produce *zōng*]. (The *Shijing* reads *sān rǎn jiàng yě*, meaning three dyes produce crimson. Five dyes produce *zēi*. Seven...
Regarding the term *zhī* (black), Master Zheng’s commentary states that it is made black by dyeing it twice;
thus, when the nun Jingxiu saw the color of the robes of the noble assembly, it was a deep blackish-red, like the color of mulberry fruit.
If there are those who sever [these defilements], they are called Bodhisattvas, called true upholders of the precepts, called worthy men (bhadra-puruṣa), and called disciples of the Buddha.
Regarding "Bodhisattva," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that "bodhi" refers to the path of the Buddha, and "sattva" refers to accomplishing sentient beings;
thus, one uses the path of the Buddhas to bring sentient beings to fulfillment. Furthermore, "bodhi" refers to one's own practice.

"Transforming others while cultivating the Buddha-way for oneself, and further using that to transform others"—the *Xianshi chao* (Notes on the Worthy Man) quotes the *Candrasūtra* (Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra), stating:
"One who is able to maintain pure precepts is called a 'superior man' (*śreṣṭha-puruṣa*). The meaning is the same as this. Regarding "disciples of the Buddha," Master Ō states:
"Because they are born from the Buddha, have obtained a portion of the Buddha-dharma, and inherit the Buddha's lineage, they are named 'Buddha-disciples' (*buddhaputra*)."
Furthermore, the *Dachao* states: "Those who study after me are called 'disciples' (*di*); those whose understanding arises from me are called 'sons' (*zi*).

Regarding the two matters of wealth and sensual pleasure, although they appear light on the surface, the offenses incurred by them are extremely grave; the delusions that deceive as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges all arise from wealth and sensual pleasure."
These two faults can destroy the relationships between ruler and minister, teacher and disciple, husband and wife, as well as internal and external kin, friends, and spiritual companions.
Their characteristics appear to be light because they consist of craving for wealth and attachment to sensual beauty; thus, their nature is not grave, appearing light like the rules of the Vinaya.
The ten kinds of black-hearted states arise in relation to matters of wealth. Furthermore, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) states:

"Although sexual desire does not afflict sentient beings, the mind remains bound and attached to it. Though this may seem like a minor transgression, as for its retribution, one shall suffer the pains of hell for nine hundred twenty-one billion sixty thousand years.
Therefore, it is said that the resulting sin is particularly grave, as in the case of the "White Tiger" incident involving the ruler and his ministers.

"Tongyunjun" (通云君) means "the lord of the commandery," the one to whom the hearts of the multitude below turn. "Chenfu" (臣伏) means "ministerial submission. "Nanren" (男子) is a humble designation for a man.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals Commentary* (*Chunqiu shuo*) states: "The orthodox qi constitutes the Emperor; the intermediate qi constitutes the ministers.

Regarding "shifu" (師父), the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhouli*) says: "A 'shi' (teacher) is a designation for one who instructs others in the Way. Furthermore, Yang Xiong stated: "A 'shi' is a person's model and standard; 'tu' (party/disciples) refers to their followers."

Regarding the roles of husband and wife, the *Dazaili* (Great Carriage Rites) states: "The husband (*fu*) is so called because he 'supports' (*fu*); it means he supports and regulates the myriad things.
Regarding the wife (*fu*), the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "She is so called because she 'serves' (*fu*); it means she serves the affairs of the household.

As for internal and external relations, those such as uncles and elder brothers are the internal kin, while maternal uncles and parents-in-law are the external kin. Regarding friends, the Preface to the *Mao Shi* says: "In place of wood, one entertains friends and old acquaintances."

From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, there are none who have not required friends to achieve completion. Furthermore, those from the same school are called *peng* (companions), while those with the same aspirations are called *you* (friends).
One who hears of one’s name and praises one’s virtue is called a *zhi* (knower); one who beholds one’s form and reverently serves is called a *shi* (cognizer).

There are generally three kinds: first, the external protector as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); second, the fellow practitioner as a spiritual friend; and third, the teacher [as a spiritual friend].
When bestowing [teachings], one must generally warn such people that their ruin does not arise from anything other than wealth and sensual desire;
therefore, they must be cautioned. The Buddha said: "Wealth and sensual desire are like a blade smeared with honey.
It is not enough to satisfy a single meal, yet if a child licks it, he will suffer the calamity of injuring his tongue. (This refers to self-inflicted harm.)
The preceding [passage] concerns harming others due to wealth and sensual pleasures.

If one is free from wealth and sensual pleasures, there is nothing further in the world of humans and devas for the sake of liberation from suffering; thus, both noble and ordinary beings alike praise the total extinction of all outflows (*āsrava*) and the advancement toward the fruit of Buddhahood.
For this reason, these two—wealth and sensual pleasures—are the primary warnings.

Furthermore, there is nothing in the world equal to this: the five aggregates of sentient beings, together with their supporting environments—the inferior retributions of both the primary and secondary bodies—are all caused by wealth and sensual desire.
If one now distances oneself from wealth and sensual desire, these inferior retributions will cease to exist. Humans and devas represent the superior states that encompass the inferior;
this applies universally across the six realms of existence for both the holy and the ordinary. Let the ordinary become worthy (賢, *xian*), and progress until the fruit of Buddhahood is attained.
Because one is not obstructed by delusions regarding sense objects, one will ultimately reach the ultimate Way. As the Buddha said:
"One who practices the Way is like a piece of wood floating in water, following the current without touching either bank;
it is not taken by people, nor obstructed by ghosts or spirits, nor held back by eddies, nor does it rot. I guarantee that it will enter [the sea]."
O Sea! Those who practice the Way are not deluded by sensual desires nor deceived by various evils;
they are diligent and unimpeded—I guarantee that such people will enter the Way.

Because of physical form one gives rise to arrogance, and because of wealth one gives rise to stinginess; though one possesses abundant virtue, if one is both arrogant and stingy, it is not worth regarding.
"Kiao" (憍) means arrogance; "lian" (憐) means indulgence. It is also originally written as "jiao" (驕) and "lin" (恡), though the correct forms are "jin" (悋) and "bi" (鄙), both meaning stinginess.
If a person possesses these two faults, even if they have other remaining virtues, those virtues are insufficient to be observed. Confucius said:

"If there were one who possessed the talent and beauty of the Duke of Zhou, yet was arrogant and stingy, his other qualities would be insufficient to be observed. Xing Bing (邢昺) stated that this means... [text continues].
This is because one has been obscured and abandoned by base stinginess.
First, sever attachment to wealth and sensual desires so that merit and practice may be established; afterwards, listen to the sutras and śāstras—this is the sequence for entering the Way.
It is said that because it proceeds against the current, it is called "purifying the mind."

The first two lines [of the verse] concern the severing [of attachments], which encompasses the Vinaya; hence it is said below that "one who can sever wealth and desire is called one who upholds the Vinaya.
Now, the Great Master’s intention is that one must first uphold the Vinaya-piṭaka and subsequently study the Sūtras and Śāstras before attaining their sequence.
As for the words "contrary to the flow," although these words may be jarring to the ear for a time, they are able to spur the practitioner on to swiftly reach the Way.
It is for this reason that it is called the "pure mind.
The verse says:
Regarding the term "verse" (gāthā), the Dharma Master Ying states that it is a transliteration of the Sanskrit. It is correctly termed *gāthā*, or alternatively *śloka*. This...
It was intended to be a *gāthā* summarizing the sutra, but it has been corrupted [into the word] "yuē" (曰). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "yuē" means "words";
it is composed of the radical for "mouth" and the phonetic "yī" (一), and its form also resembles breath issuing from the mouth. Thus, "yuē" is a particle used to introduce speech.
Afflictions are like the sands of the Ganges; first, sever the two kinds of evil. First is wealth, the second is form;
at the time of death, the spirit will have no fear. One must guard against even a *duṣkṛta* offense; how much more so when one has committed the four grave offenses?
When the threefold aggregate of precepts is pure, the mind leaps with joy during the *poṣadha*.

"River sands" refers to the sands of the Ganges River; this river is eighty *yojanas* long and forty *yojanas* wide, its bottom is extremely deep so that elephants sink completely when crossing it, and its sand is as fine as flour while its water is white as milk.
This is now used as a metaphor for the abundance of afflictions (*kleśa*). "The spirit is not afraid" means that by severing these two [afflictions], one reaches the end of life.
Ultimately, one’s consciousness will have no fear or timidity. Conversely, if one does not maintain this continuity, one will harbor fear at the time of death;
"duṣkṛta" (吉羅) refers to the minor offenses among the five categories of transgressions. Regarding the correct phonetics according to the *Śabdavidyā*, it is *dukkaṭa*;
the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* calls it *śikṣākaraṇīya*. Its meaning is translated as "that which should be learned. Indian monks say it means "guarding the precepts," for this offense is subtle.
This means to study and observe them minutely. Now, by encouraging the protection of the small [precepts], one is cautioned regarding the great; hence it is said, "How much more so" (*kai-gwan*).

The violation of the four grave offenses refers to the three clusters of precepts (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*), which are the Mahāyāna precepts. First is the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint): this means being free from all evil and initiating the practice that realizes the Way;
it is the cause for the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) and results in the formation of the *dharmakāya*. The *Yingluo jing* (Sutra of the Jeweled Necklace) states: "The *vinaya*..."
Regarding the precepts of ritual conduct (*samvara-śīla*), the *Bodhisattva-śīla-vṛtti* states that the precept of restraining the mind (*saṃvara-śīla*) enables the mind to abide [in concentration].
Regarding the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), it means there is no good that is not gathered;

this refers to the virtues of body, speech, and mind, as well as the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation—the six *pāramitās*, and the eighty-four thousand practices that assist the path. These constitute the cause for cultivating the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
The *Sūtra on the Ornament of the Reward Body* states: "Gathering wholesome dharmas" refers to the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates. The *Commentary on the Precepts* says:

"By gathering wholesome dharmas, one spontaneously accomplishes the Buddha-dharma. The third is the precept of gathering sentient beings, also known as the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-śīla*).

This means that there are no beings not saved, giving rise to the non-abiding path; this is the cause of its benevolent virtue. Through cultivation, it is perfected as the ornament of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The Sūtra says: "Gathering in sentient beings" refers to transforming them through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), causing them to attain peace and happiness.

The *Śīla-śāstra* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "Gathering in sentient beings" means bringing sentient beings to maturity. The *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha-alaṃkāra-śāstra* says: "The first precept has restraint as its essence;
the latter two precepts have diligence as their essence. *Poṣadha*—here translated as "Pure Abiding"—is the essential path of deliverance.
The *Vinaya* says it is the language of the kingdom of Kośala. Regarding the six fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa*, "poṣadha" has two meanings:
first, dwelling in pure precepts; second, increasing merit. Now, because the precepts are pure and merit increases, the mind is joyful and courageous.
The base person displays a [pleased] countenance when there is affection; I admonish you to sever greedy attachment.

Because wealth is the cause of suffering throughout the three periods of time, one enters a fire-pot due to form—the vulgar and lowly nature of "affection" refers to the mind of greedy defilement, which is called "affection" (愛) regarding all wealth and forms.

Because of this attachment, it belongs to the affliction of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Regarding the "two periods," these are the present and the future; the past is not mentioned because it has already passed away.
Due to causes in the present life, such as seeking wealth and sensual pleasures, one undergoes exhaustion, or the suffering of not obtaining what is sought;
even if one does obtain them, when pleasure reaches its peak, it declines and the characteristics of suffering manifest, continuing until the end of life.
Because they undergo the suffering of mud and mire, the subsequent line says, "entering fire jars and cauldrons due to form.
This refers to the instruments of torment in the Avīci Hell. The *Fayuan zhulin* states: "The boiling cauldrons surge with waves, and the flaming furnaces rise up."
Form can obstruct the Noble Path; wealth can cause one's practice to become thin. Examine your own mind with discernment:
know that craving is a deluded error.
Regarding "form obstructing the Path," the *Mahāsāṃghika* states that because one violates this precept, one has no share in the fruits of the Path. In the Vinaya, this refers to sexual misconduct.
Desire is the primary concern; it is because the Buddha wished for bhikṣus to attain nirvāṇa in this very life that he caused the practice of wealth to become thin.
This is because when one is greedy for wealth, conduct characterized by high integrity gradually diminishes. The *Mahā-śāstra* says: "Greed for worldly profit destroys the merit of the Path;
the loss of wealth causes the loss of the laypeople's heart of faith and respect, and furthermore, it violates the Buddha’s Four Reliances and is not a matter of integrity."

Frugal conduct is the mark of one who knows the face of the Great Being; the Heavenly Subhūti was ranked as having the highest capacity, yet he ultimately returned to being a vessel of the lower grade.

If even Yanzi still found joy in his single ladle of water, how much more so for those who have transcended the world—would they instead allow themselves to be hindered at the very start of their journey by wealth and profit?

The wise avoid [sensual desires] as if they were fiery pits, while the stubborn and ignorant do not find them loathsome; if one commits an offense, one should repent and eliminate it, and having eliminated it, one must not do it again.
The *Teaching Left Behind* (Yizu jing) says that those who possess wisdom avoid wealth and sensual desire as if they were fiery pits.

One should distance oneself from all wealth and treasures as one would avoid a pit of fire. Master Aśvaghoṣa’s commentary explains that this is because it is analogous to avoiding a great mass of fire.
The phrase "obstinate" (wán) is the opposite of the preceding line; it means that fools do not detest [wealth] because they do not recognize it as a calamity.
Regarding the word "if" (ruò): the Buddha said there are two kinds of wise people: first, those who do not commit [offenses]; second, those who, having committed them, [repent].
One who can repent for the present and exhorts others to repent for the past may still be called wise; yet one who commits transgressions and does not reform them is even more foolish.
All things that possess form ultimately end up filling the ditches and ravines. By maintaining the precepts and restraining the mind from suffering, one will later receive great peace and joy.
In the end, it returns below; once the physical form has perished, it is no longer an object of affection, for it ultimately fills the ditches and pits.
The *Zhangfu yi* states: "The physical forms of a single lifetime are cast into ditches and ravines, while the spiritual essences of successive generations are bound to the path of karma.
This meaning is the same. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "A 'gou' (ditch) is a water channel, wide and deep."

"Four chi deep" (*sìchǐ hè*): the *Erya* states that when flowing water becomes deep, it forms a ravine; it also refers to a ditch or pond, and furthermore, a pit. Regarding "maintaining the precepts":
if one uses the maintenance of the precepts to restrain the passions of craving for wealth and lustful desire, then one will not undergo the sufferings of the two worlds (present and future).
Therefore, one obtains three kinds of happiness in the near term and proceeds toward Nirvana in the distant term. The hidden intention lies in the distant goal.
This refers to "Greatness.

The third section on the method of the Five Contemplations for Stilling the Mind (Pañca-nīvaraṇa-pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) provides a threefold explanation of the five categories of stilling. These two types of coarse defilements are distanced so as to serve as the fundamental principle for entering the Path; thus, they are regulated across five points.

Because taking the mind as one's guide is the foundation of superior practice, this chapter is established following the preceding stage. It is said that since the three poisons and arrogance cause distraction, one should cultivate their cessation;

thus, the five methods of settling the mind (*pañca-vinodana-citta*) are called "stopping" (*śamatha*), while the systematic examination and treatment [of these afflictions] is termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the five types of deluded conceptualization: just as one removes a thorny tree by first cutting its roots, one cultivates the five stabilizing contemplations (*pañca-vinodana*) to pacify the five faults;
because they prevent these faults from arising, they are called "stabilizing mind contemplations" (*sthāpanā-citta-bhāvanā*).

The five delusions are greed, hatred, ignorance, pride, and distraction. The "thorny tree" refers to trees with thorns and brambles, which serve as a metaphor for the various subtle afflictions and hindrances.
To eliminate these hindrances, one must first cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to remove the five types of coarse faults at their root.
The method for removing them consists of the five *sthāpanā*. *Sthāpanā* means "to cause to abide. That is to say, one performs...
At the time of this contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one halts the mind at five points and reflects with observation;

"halting" (*sthāpanā*) is also said to mean "resting," because it means resting the afflictions and so forth. As for "contemplation," it refers to the mental sovereign (*manovijñāna*) associated with wisdom (*prajñā*), which seeks out and observes;
therefore, it is called contemplation.

By practicing this contemplation, present afflictions cease to arise, and one attains minor liberation; the basis for this is the gradual realization of supernormal powers through the flexibility of ethical discipline and meditative concentration, which is called "great liberation.

The total extinction of the ten obstacles is called "true liberation. All of these are not possible without relying on the five methods of cessation and contemplation (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-pratipakṣa*) practiced in this way;
thus, such entry into practice is termed "purifying the mind."
Those who currently manifest afflictions do not act upon them because they have been suppressed; yet, as these have not yet been truly severed, it is said that they have attained "minor liberation.
This is because "by" (you) means "due to," "following from," or "caused by. "Supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) generally encompasses the six *abhijñās*.

Because delusions are not yet exhausted and realization is not yet ultimate, it is called "gradual"; only when the delusions of views and thought are exhausted and the fruit of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*) is realized is it [truly so] named.

Furthermore, because liberation is relatively small compared to what precedes it, it receives the designation "Great. Regarding the ten obstacles, these refer to the fact that within each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one obstacle is destroyed.
This is similar to how the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) speaks of destroying eleven types of obstacles upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Moreover, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, the obstacle to the Buddha-stage is severed, whereby one enters the Sublime.
Awakening is what is truly called liberation. Thus, both the great and small fruits do not fail to take the five *sthāpanā-cittas* as the initial gateway for entering the Path.
The verse says:
Knowing for oneself that sensual desire is great, one should single-mindedly contemplate the impure. Through renunciation, one attains liberation;
when desire is exhausted, one immediately attains concentration. If one pursues discursive debate, the thought of desire will only grow more intense;
this is not the remedy, but a downward path leading into a perilous track.

Regarding the subduing of sensual desire: sentient beings who are dominated by craving for the objects of desire are instructed by the Buddha to practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as an antidote.
Although the objects of craving are numerous, they do not exceed four types: first, color (*varṇa*; blue, yellow, red, white); second, shape (*saṃsthāna*; long, short, square, round);
third, exquisite touch (*sparśa*; the smoothness and softness of the body); and fourth, service (*paricaryā*; attendance and devotion). There are likewise four methods of treatment: first, blue...

1. The perception of a bloated corpse (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*)—which treats the greed for color; 2. The perception of a festering corpse (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*)—which treats the greed for shape; 3. The perception of a worm-infested corpse (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*)—which treats the greed for exquisite touch; 4. The perception of a corpse (*vikhāditaka-saṃjñā*)—which treats the greed for honor and service.
The *Abhidharmakośa* treats these as a single "contemplation of the skeleton" (*asthi-śaṅkalikā-vipaśyanā*), which universally counteracts all four types of greed.

Regarding the two subsequent phrases concerning the benefits of the "liberations" (*vimokṣa*), they should be explained sequentially. As for the phrase "the discourse [belongs to] the distracted mind," it means that the teaching pertains to the state of a scattered mind and has not yet reached [the stage of] meditative concentration.

When one attempts to defend against them, sensual desires instead flare up even more intensely; the essential point lies in cultivating the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as an antidote.
The *Xiangfa jueyi jing* clarifies the faults of Dharma masters, stating that they merely seek external textual explanations without internally contemplating and cultivating the mind.
It further says: "Without dhyāna there is no wisdom; with wisdom alone and no dhyāna, it is like a bird with only one wing or a wheel with only one rim—how could such a thing travel far?"
The metaphor of directing one’s mindfulness downward through a perilous path illustrates how merely pursuing discursive debate causes the loss of contemplative practice.

Recognizing for yourself that anger is prevalent, Dedicate yourself exclusively to the cultivation of loving-kindness and compassion. Thus the fire of poison will attain coolness, and you will achieve the excellence of ethical discipline.
If you instead pursue scholarly discourse, It is not a remedy; it is but a wearying labor in vain.
Greed and hatred further increase, and one is heavily bound by afflictions (*kleśa*).
For those sentient beings who are prone to anger, one should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*) as an antidote;

this should be applied to enemies, kin, and neutral parties (dividing enemies and kin each into three grades, plus the neutral, making seven). One should then bestow the three kinds of happiness (the bliss of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and devas) equally upon them. From...
To transform the difficult into the easy so that those of the seven grades may all obtain the three joys is to achieve equanimity of mind.

If this contemplation is perfected, the poison-fire of hatred is immediately dispelled; because a hateful mind is parched and hot, it is like fire, yet through the application of contemplation, it is extinguished and one attains coolness.
If one acts below by emulating what was done above, the same principle applies to what follows, as illustrated in the "Biographies of Eminent Monks" (Xu gaoseng zhuan).
Tong said: "Mingchen was a man of Qi who traveled to study in Xihe during his youth; he gained renown for his mastery of the *Zhuangzi*.

Although he possessed a rich knowledge of the sūtras and śāstras, he was particularly intent on posing challenges and objections. He once composed the *She-re-lun* (Treatise on the Snake’s Heat), which was like Zhuge Liang’s battle formation known as the 'Eternal Coiling Snake' (*chang-shan she-shi*).
During the final years of the Daye era, there were many scholars; subsequently, because a monk in Luzhou preached the *Lotus Sūtra*..."
Sengchen requested a trial debate; the monk, knowing that Sengchen’s discourse on the Way was difficult to withstand, informed him of his true feelings and presented him with fourteen rolls of silk.
Sengchen accepted them but did not depart, wishing instead to attend a single lecture. This monk was so anxious that he could not help himself and proceeded as usual to expound the text.
Later, Sengchen entered the hall and, holding the silk before the assembly, said: "Yesterday, the Dharma Master on the high seat..."
He left behind silk as an offering, requesting that no further debate be held; however, since the Buddha-dharma is vast and profound, right and wrong must be distinguished.
At that time, Sengchao’s spirit was bold and vigorous, and he waited with composure for challenges, answering every successive difficulty without fail.
Sengbin’s mind was in turmoil, and as he struggled to find a way to counter the arguments, he thought, "Master Gaoseng has always been obscure and obstructed; how is it that today—"
"An instantaneous realization such as this must surely be the aid of the divine," they said, and the entire assembly laughed heartily.

Daochen then left the town with his two companions to seek alms at their homes; his mind and breath were so choked with emotion that he could not swallow. Although his companions tried to console him, he sighed and lamented at every step.
Reaching the summit of a ridge, utterly exhausted, he stopped beneath a single tree and immediately began to strip off his clothes until he was stark naked.
While lying down, he moved his body again and said to his companion, "I am now afflicted with a mental state that desires to become a snake;
first I manifested the posture of a snake, and now its retribution has arrived. You must climb a tree; if the snake-heart reaches me, there will be the danger of being devoured.
Having finished speaking, his entire body transformed into a snake about fifty feet long, and he rushed down the valley. His companion witnessed this with his own eyes.
Upon arriving in Ye, he preached this: "Those with greed and anger—'greed' should perhaps be 'should' (令), for greed belongs to the preceding category of what is to be remedied;
it is not a word to be recorded [as a primary fault].
One knows for oneself that delusion is great; by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one first realizes the suffering of saṃsāra."

Having realized the non-existence of self and person, if one should pursue mere discursive debate, one will see contention and clamor all day long, abandoning the root to seek after branches and leaves;
thus one cannot uproot the ignorance that lies at the base.
For those sentient beings who are dominated by delusion, one should cause them to practice the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination as an antidote.
The twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) refer to the twelve factors, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*).

They are taught in terms of the causes and effects of the three periods of time to remedy the delusions regarding those three periods. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states, they are explained as the prior, middle, and subsequent limits in order to dispel the ignorance and confusion of others.

This means that explaining the prior limit dispels ignorance regarding the past (namely, the two factors of ignorance and volitional formations), while explaining the subsequent limit dispels ignorance regarding the future (namely, birth and old age and death).

Regarding the "limb of death," it is taught that the delusion concerning the middle period [of existence] is dispelled by the eight limbs—consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and becoming.

Within this, there are two modes of contemplation: the forward and the reverse. The forward contemplation proceeds from ignorance to old age and death, namely: "Because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease," and so forth.

The reverse contemplation proceeds from old age and death back to ignorance, namely: "The limb of old age and death ceases because the limb of birth ceases," and so forth. Thus, through these causes, the delusions regarding the present are eliminated.

This can then counteract the disease of ignorance; "beginning to realize" (始悟) also refers to the benefit arising from realization. Because of this realization, one does not undergo the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).

If transmigration is extinguished, then there are no views of self, person, or sentient beings, nor is there contention. "Contention" refers to the matter of not manifesting debates through the clashing of lips and tongues.
To let go of the root is to not cultivate the observation of causes and conditions regarding the branches and leaves.
If one pursues discursive debate, it is like a fool regarding the sense bases;
knowing for oneself that pride is great, one must carefully contemplate the eighteen elements. Only then can one realize there is no person, and the illness of the self will be cured.
If one continues to pursue discursive debate, it will instead increase the debts of the three miserable realms.
I constantly seek victory, yet fame and profit are my own shackles.
Beneath pride, one becomes attached to a self; thus, one should practice the contemplation of the differentiation of the realms of sentient beings as a remedy for this self-clinging.
"Self" (ātman) is defined by the sense of being a sovereign master; because sentient beings do not understand that the physical body is empty and false, they falsely imagine it to exist.
Because of attachment to a self, pride arises; therefore, one should contemplate that the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) exist merely as provisional conditions.

Within this, those of sharp faculties contemplate six elements, while those of dull faculties contemplate all eighteen elements as being deluded regarding many phenomena—namely, the six external objects, the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*), and the six consciousness elements. When the practitioner contemplates thus...
The six internal sense-bases (āyatana) have only the meaning of being the basis for growth;
the six external objects have only the meaning of drawing the mind toward their respective conditions; and the six consciousness-elements have only the meaning of perceiving and discerning.
If this contemplation is perfected, one will realize that the sovereign self has no further locus to which it can be attributed. Thus, one awakens to the fact that [the self] is utterly non-existent.
Therefore I say that only when one attains the state of being "without a person" will the illness of clinging to a self naturally be cured.

Shackles and fetters— *zhì* (shackles on the feet) and *gù* (fetters on the hands)— are metaphors for the two kinds of worldly gain and fame (*mínglì*) which confine a person and prevent them from finding ease and leisure.
Knowing for oneself that discursive thoughts are many, One should constantly count the inhalations and exhalations.
When vitarka and vicāra gradually achieve the power of concentration, If one instead pursues lectures and debates, The clamor and dust of the world cannot be stilled;
As they alternately dispute right and wrong, When will the consciousness of phenomena ever cease?

Regarding "disordered thoughts" (*vikalpa*) below: those with many discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*) are also called "distracted beings" (*vikṣipta-sattva*) and also called "beings of investigation and analysis" (*vitarka-vicāra-sattva*).
The Buddha taught the practice of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) as an antidote; this will be clarified in detail later in this very text.

As for the phrase "gradually attaining accomplishment" (*kramaśo niṣpatti-labdha*), the character "accomplishment" (*cheng*) is an error and should be "extinguished" (*mie*). Through *vitarka* and *vicāra*, [the breath] is gradually extinguished.

These are vitarka (Sanskrit: *vitarka*; Chinese: *xún*) and vicāra (Sanskrit: *vicāra*; Chinese: *sì*). Vitarka is translated as "investigation" (*xún*), and vicāra is translated as "analysis" (*sì*).

The old translations render them as "awakening" (*jué*) and "observation" (*guān*). The *Abhidharmasaṃyuktavastu-śāstra* states: "If the mind operates diffusely and arises repeatedly, this is called awakening (*vitarka*);
when the diffused mind is slightly subtle, it is called observation (*vicāra*"). These two dharmas pervade all three realms.

The coarseness and subtlety of this mind are illustrated by the striking of a bell: the initial sound is *vitarka* (initial application), and the subsequent resonance is *vicāra* (sustained application).

If one adds the lower stages of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), and if distraction arises, it is immediately extinguished; thus, because morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are all preeminent, they possess power.
Regarding the phrase "reciprocally," etc.: one regards oneself as right and disparages others as wrong, claiming to hold the jewel of the divine serpent (*nāga*).
It is like carrying the jade of Mount Jing. Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it teaches that there are three kinds of consciousness (*vijñāna*):

the true consciousness (the Tathāgatagarbha), the manifesting consciousness (the eighth consciousness), and the consciousness of discriminating phenomena (the first six consciousnesses). Furthermore, because the sixth consciousness alone is designated as the "consciousness of phenomena," the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda Śāstra* states:
"That which follows after objects, grasps at conditions, and discriminates the six sense-fields is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It is also thus.
It is called the "consciousness of separation" and is also termed the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena. The Master of the *Ālaya* explains:

because it is able to discriminate the various characteristics of phenomena—past and future, internal and external—this refers to the first of the seven stages of skillful means (*saptavidha-upāya*) within the Abhidharma, namely the attainment of the name through the five contemplations (*pañca-viṣkambhanā-vipaśyanā*). All other [stages] are...

The specific-characteristics mindfulness establishments (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*), the general-characteristics mindfulness establishments (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*), the stage of warmth (*uṣmagata*), the stage of summits (*mūrdhan*), the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) are called the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*).

When these contemplative practices are perfected, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*). Whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna practitioners, all who first enter the Path cultivate this contemplation.
*Abhidharma* (also called *Vibhāṣā*, *Abhidharma*, or *Abhidhamma*) is a transliteration of a Sanskrit term;

it means "Superior Dharma" (*abhi-dharma*) or "Incomparable Dharma," so named because it characterizes wisdom (*prajñā*), and thus refers to the treatises (*śāstra*). Regarding the "seven stages of application" (*saptaprayoga*):

"application" (*prayoga*) here carries the sense of "cause," as these stages all serve as the means for attaining the subsequent fruit; they are also termed the "seven worthies" (*sapta-ārya*) in contrast to what follows.
Regarding the "distinct characteristics" of the four noble truths: "distinct" means that the body, mind, and dharmas are each different from one another;
it refers to contemplating these four dharmas through such mental modes as the perception of impurity (*aśubha*). As for "mindfulness" (*smṛti*), its essential nature is clear recollection.

Since the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) is volatile, mindfulness is now employed to memorize and fixate upon the object so that it is not forgotten. Regarding the "general characteristic" mindfulness, the practitioner contemplates...

As one gradually becomes proficient, in a single moment one comprehensively contemplates the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena as suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self (the three stages above belong to the outer ordinary stage of the *sambhāra-mārga*). Regarding the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage: it is named after a metaphor;

just as a person approaching a fire perceives the precursor signs of fire, so too is the arising of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) called "Heat," for it is able to burn away the fuel of delusions regarding the nature of reality.
Regarding "Heat" (*uṣmagata*): although this has not yet arisen, it is called "Heat" because it is the precursor to the fire of the wisdom already attained.

Regarding the meditative cultivation practiced at this stage, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "From this arises the Dharma of Heat, which fully contemplates the Four Noble Truths and cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
As for the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), there is a wholesome root that follows the superior grade of the wholesome root of Heat.
Birth is named "Summit" (*mūrdhan*); "Summit" carries the meaning of reaching the ultimate. There are two interpretations of this:
first, it is said that while the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summit are subject to regression and fluctuation, the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) is free from regression and fluctuation.

Thus, the stage of Summit reaches the point of non-regression—the ultimate limit, the ultimate place—just as the crown of a person's head is the ultimate part of the body. Second, it is said that the stage of Heat is only... [text ends]
The stage of patience (*kṣānti*) consists solely of progress; this present stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), however, is the midpoint between progress and retreat.

Like the peak of a mountain situated between the two sides of above and below, it is therefore called the "summit. Regarding the meditative cultivation practiced at this stage, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"Next, the summit is likewise produced," meaning that one contemplates the four truths in the same manner as before, performing them as a single [unit].
The sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) are also present here; however, this stage is merely more advanced. Regarding the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*):

following the roots of goodness of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), there arises a root of goodness called Patience. This Patience has two meanings: first, the meaning of "sealing" (*anumodana*), because it is able to seal the principle of the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya*);
second, the meaning of "certainty" (*niścaya*), because it is able to determine [the truth] such that there is no further regression or wavering. In this stage...

In the practice of contemplative cultivation (*vipaśyanā*), during the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), one contemplates the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the Four Noble Truths; during "middle patience" (*madhya-kṣānti*), there are seven cycles of reducing the objects (*ālambana*) and twenty-four cycles of reducing the aspects;
during "upper patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one contemplates only a single aspect of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the desire realm for a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* verse states: "Lower and middle patience are the same as the Peak [of the Worldly Path]; upper patience contemplates only one aspect of the suffering of the desire realm for a single moment."
That which follows the roots of goodness known as "patience" (kṣānti) is called the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma).

This refers to the fact that for this practitioner, within the state of a worldly ordinary person (pṛthagjana) characterized by outflows (sāsrava), this stage is the most supreme. Consequently, the contemplative practice cultivated at this stage is identical to that of the stage of patience;
it consists solely of contemplating the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) in a single aspect and for a single moment.
Because it serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) that introduces one to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"The Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*) are likewise [the cause]. (The above four stages belong to the stage of application for those within the ranks of the ordinary person). *Srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer): This is translated as "逆流" (*ni-liu*,逆流, "flowing against the current"). Having already severed the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of seeing (*darśana-heya*), one first perceives the True Truth (*satya*).

Because one flows against the current of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one is also called "預流" (*yu-liu*, 預流, "entering the stream"). One has initially entered the stream of the Noble Ones (*ārya-srota*).
Therefore, the verse says:
For what reason are the five remedies taught? Why do you not follow the lecture on the sutras? You are like one who, while suffering from an illness, merely recites the prescriptions for medicine.

Seeking only fame and reputation, The worldling craves gain and offerings. Without intent to cure or forget worldly attachments, If one practices the five contemplations (*pañca-vipaśyanā*), One will certainly achieve success in cultivating the Path.
[The final two lines are to be inferred from what precedes: What cause lies above? Embracing illness, the [final] four lines praise not pursuing lectures and treatises.

Therefore, to forget emotions and forget activity is to act delusively; if one cultivates the latter two lines of the verse, one will gain benefit from the five cessations (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-pratipakṣa*).
This shows that much talk is not as good as little practice; to exert oneself in virtue is what is supreme.
For what reason does it cause one to cultivate the five methods of stabilizing meditation (*pañca-vastu-pratipakṣa*) and cease pursuing discursive debate?

For what reason? The interrogative phrasing below has the same meaning as the preceding verse; this [verse] should have been placed above in the prose (*gadya*), while the verse below should have been made a re-verse (*geya*).
It seems that later scribes, fearing confusion, may have erroneously transposed the remedies.
There are two essential dharmas: first, the sequential entry into the path according to the Buddha’s teachings as an antidote to coarse and heavy afflictions;

second, those who, though knowing the principles of the Dharma, intentionally transgress them out of disregard for the Buddha’s precepts, failing to cultivate dignified deportment, and utterly destroying the pure precepts of the five categories.
Upon seeing others uphold the precepts, they further give rise to hatred and slander; they crave wealth and beauty, and are consumed by anger, vexation, and strife.
Those who harbor contention, stinginess, envy, pride, lack of shame, and lack of remorse will, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, inevitably fall into the realms of hell,

animals, or hungry ghosts, remaining there for many kalpas; one should contemplate this matter and verify it through present experience, thereby practicing the five cessations to stop transgressions and give rise to the Path,
following the Buddha’s teaching— this is called "purifying the mind."

Regarding the "coarse and heavy afflictions," these refer to the aforementioned five faults such as greed; because they are countered by the five meditative cessations (*pañca-smṛtyupasthāna*), one is exhorted to cultivate them.
Furthermore, the reason for prohibiting discursive debate is that those who preach the Dharma often do so for the sake of fame and profit, and because they knowingly commit offenses.
The five categories of offenses—*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *duṣkṛta*—are as follows: [the text continues with the specific definitions].

It is said that those possessing the three "Equilibrations" (sāmya) are called "Chapters" (pāda), while those lacking them are termed "Clusters" (saṃgraha). The Master [Vasubandhu] does not hold this view;

even if a "Cluster" follows the five stages (*pañca-vastuka*), it possesses the meaning of the three "Equilibrations. Although the name "Chapter" appears in the seven original texts, because its meaning is subsumed within the "Miscellaneous," there is nothing that cannot be manifested.

"Verification" (*pratyakṣa*) refers to verifying cause and effect. The term "chai-lang" (豺狼) should correctly be written as "chai-lang" (豺狼); it belongs to the category [of animals] mentioned in the *Liji* (Book of Rites).
It is said that in the month of late autumn, the jackals sacrifice their prey. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that they resemble dogs with pointed heads and white cheeks;

they are tall in the front and broad in the rear. They are by nature excessively greedy and gluttonous (*Wang Yi’s commentary on the *Chuci* says: "to love wealth is greed; to love food is gluttony").
The verse says:
Greed has the nature of a jackal or wolf; hatred has the mind of an evil dragon. Because they destroy the Dharma, they violate prohibitions, defile precepts, and commit lewdness.
Though one recognizes the Dharma and hopes to eliminate its poison, one instead commits even deeper transgressions.
Having committed karma without remorse, one passes away and approaches the forest of blades, falling into the Great Avīci Hell;
the Buddha-nature sinks for kalpas like a dismissed official punished and stripped of power, rendered incapable of fulfilling his duties.
Regarding the "evil dragon": the dragon is the sovereign of scaly creatures; because its mind abounds in the poison of anger, it is now taken as the second [example].
"Analogies" (lei) refers to similes; "evil" (jian) is a vulgar corruption of "private misconduct" (si). "Sword Forest" (Dao-lin) refers to the instruments of retribution in hell. The *Fayuan* states:

"The Sword Forest towers toward the sun and the Ridge of Swords reaches the heavens. As for "Buddha-nature" (foxing), it is the single, true enlightened nature inherently possessed by all sentient beings.
Because of the commission of offenses through transgression, one falls into the cycle of suffering, like an official [losing his position].

The *Baibhutong* says: "Each measures their office and exhausts their talent. This means that when high officials, such as dukes, ministers, and grandees, have committed offenses while in office, they are stripped of their titles and punished;
this serves as a metaphor for sentient beings who, though endowed with Buddha-nature, nevertheless fall into the cycle of suffering due to their transgressions.
How is it that with a mouth of broken precepts one greedily devours the food of others? How is it that with hands of broken precepts one receives the gifts of wealth and property from others?
How is it that because of these lower forms of broken precepts, both wealth and the Dharma are lost? As the *Buddhapiṭaka* states: "One who does not eliminate the inversion of self-grasping..."
One does not even accept a single cup of water or a single patchwork robe, much less indulge in receiving the abundant benefits of faithful offerings.

How can one with a body that has broken the precepts sit or lie upon fine beds and cushions? How can one whose actions have broken the precepts receive the prostrations of others as sufficient for oneself?
Regarding fine beds and mattresses: nowadays, those who are unworthy lie upon ornate beds with thick cushions as they please, yet show not the slightest trace of shame.
Furthermore, for instance, when Prince Bodhi invited the Buddha, he had garments spread step by step on the stairs so that the Buddha might tread upon them;
however, the World-Honored One did not accept this and had him remove them, for the sake of future generations. How much more so, then, [in the present case]?
To violate the pure precepts and yet rashly accept the great sūtras—this is what is meant by the saying, "It would be better to lie upon an iron bed.

One should reflect on these words. Regarding the nature of the karma of breaking the precepts, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that this karma is fulfilled at the third *karmavācanā*. This refers to the essential substance of the karma.
What is the practice of breaking the precepts? It refers to silently accepting praise while extolling those who practice the precepts.
Because one extensively accepts and follows these two types of precepts, yet fails to achieve skillful accomplishment through external restraint, it is called "precept practice.
Since one is currently unable to fully protect them, it is termed "breaking. One should know that the former was based on the essence of the undertaking, whereas this concerns the subsequent conduct.
Regarding the practice of silently accepting the lower Vinaya rules: if there is a transgression, one must disclose it so that the assembly may fully know of it.
Now, to remain silent in such matters would mean that people would regard one as a person of pure character; thus, there are instances of receiving praise for this reason.
If one commits these five matters, all the devas will together lament them.
These five matters refer to the verbal, manual, and bodily actions [of the precepts].
When the Buddha taught those newly receiving the precepts, they were to study the Vinaya for five years before studying the Sūtras. Regarding the Vinaya, there are five schools: one and four.

It is divided into two, five, thirty, four *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, and five liberations; these five sections of the Vinaya share the same *vinaya* and its great canon (*piṭaka*), and because their textual characteristics are so vast and extensive, they are difficult to fully comprehend.
Regarding "Vinaya" (律), the Sanskrit term is *vinaya*, which translates in meaning as "discipline" (律). "Discipline" (*lǜ*) refers to the Dharma;

it is that which measures out the relative weight of what is legal and what is not, and what is determinate and what is indeterminate. Because the Dharma possesses this capacity, it is used to explain the Sūtras.

Regarding "Sūtra" (修多羅), the Sanskrit is *sūtra*, correctly translated as "thread" (線); its meaning is "affinity scripture" (契經). A thread can string together flowers, and a scripture can maintain the warp; thus it is so called.
The meaning [of "sūtra"] is like warp-threads or floral patterns; the words that can express it are able to sustain and penetrate it.

Following this convention of the local classics and edicts, it is therefore designated as a "sūtra" (jīng). Although we here mention only "sūtra" and "vinaya," they encompass the "śāstra" (treatise) as well;

for the three trainings of precepts, concentration, and wisdom must all be fully possessed. Furthermore, since the śāstra serves as the fundamental principle for interpreting the sūtras and vinayas, its meaning is also inherently contained therein.

Regarding the five schools: one hundred years after the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, the disciples of the Kaurukullaka school vied with one another to collect the texts of the Mahāsāṃghika and compile them into their own sectarian scriptures.

The *Dharmaguptaka* (the school currently followed by our tradition), the *Mahīśāsaka*, the *Sarvāstivāda*, and the *Mahāsāṃghika*—the latter being the fundamental school—are not among the five sects that emerged during the century [following the Buddha’s passing].

The *Vimukti-vinaya* (the Kāśyapīya school; this contains a *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*), the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, and the *Bahuśrutīya-vinaya* have not yet been translated because they were not transmitted [to China].

Therefore, they are not listed here; however, since the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is currently used, it is included in this count. Thus, it is concluded that these five schools of Vinaya are the same as the following five schools.
Although they differ in their specific divisions, they all belong to one great *Vinaya-piṭaka*. It is difficult to definitively determine which is the "lower" when referring to the Vinaya.
