and fourth, contemplation, as extensively elucidated in the *Ānāpāna-sūtra*.
You should receive and practice this to perfect the faculties of morality and concentration; when the nature of these faculties becomes clear and sharp, it is called the "pure mind.
One who receives and practices this contemplates the superior gate of contemplation on sensation and applies themselves diligently.

By means of this counting of breaths, one can establish the foundation for pure morality and all meditative concentrations; furthermore, when deluded thoughts and a distracted mind do not arise, this is the nature of the faculty itself.
Because it is clear and sharp, this is called a pure mind.
The verse says:
The Dharma practiced by ordinary beings on the path can only be known by the mind itself; to speak of it hastily to others—
He will instead give rise to slander; observe carefully that few words are spoken.
A person who values virtue can gather a distant multitude and draw near to a quiet place.

Sitting upright in right reflection—these four lines for the ordinary person admonish internal cultivation and must not be proclaimed outwardly; if proclaimed outwardly, others may not believe it and will thus cause slander.
As for slander, even if one has truly attained the Path according to the Vinaya, it is not permitted to proclaim it to others;

how much more so for one who has not yet attained it, which constitutes a great falsehood and defamation. Contemplate the following four lines as an admonition for those practicing meditative concentration to minimize speech.
Regarding "staying far from the multitude," the *Śāsanāntima-dharma-sūtra* states: "One should abandon one's own group and other groups, dwelling alone in seclusion to contemplate cessation."
The root of suffering is this:
merely observe your own bodily conduct; do not speak of the faults of others. Bind your tongue and speak little; remain silent with a supple mind.
Be like one who lacks knowledge, as if deaf and blind; let inner wisdom harbor the true treasure.
The dhūta practitioner delights in seclusion and tranquility; practicing in tandem with this, they remain free from indolence.
They simply observe their own body—meaning they contemplate only the conduct of their own person. If it is correct, they apply themselves even more earnestly;
if it is not correct, they should follow what is correct. This is the very foundation of self-cultivation. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one sees..."
Since he would not even speak of another’s faults as they truly are, much less slander them, Ma Yuan admonished his descendants, saying:
"I wish for you all to hear of others' transgressions as you would hear the names of your own parents—what may be heard with the ears, but must not be spoken with the mouth.
One should share in the sorrows of others and rejoice in their joys, keeping one's tongue tied; as the *Wenxuan* says: "The gong is struck."
"Tongues tied" means that one's speech is diminished; "gentle and supple" means being free from coarseness and arrogance. This admonishes the mental karma:
do not give rise to ignorant, false perceptions or wisdom, but remain like one who is deaf or blind. Cause your wisdom to be pure and your inner substance to be like one carrying precious treasures.
It is also as the Master Lao said: "Therefore, the sage empties his mind [so that it is not occupied by objects of desire]..."

If there is disorder, one is empty. Fill the belly: when the Way and its Virtue are filled within, there is no self-aggrandizement or compliance. *Dhūta* (as translated in the *Shanjian lun*) means "shaking off," referring to shaking off afflictions and departing from all attachments.
These combine to form four positions (regarding clothing, food, dwelling, and deportment), which expand into twelve.

Within clothing, two are established: the patched robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and the three robes (*tricīvara*). Within food, four are established: begging for food (*piṇḍapāta*), not performing the *atiriktabhojana-vidhi*, eating in a single sitting (*ekāsana-bhakṣa*), and eating in a single morsel (*kavaḍa-bhakṣa*). Regarding...

Regarding the five postures (*īryāpatha*)—standing, sitting in a charnel ground, sitting at the foot of a tree, sitting in the open air, and sitting wherever one happens to be—one posture is established: constant sitting (*naiṣadyika*). This refers to the "place" mentioned here;
the subsequent phrase serves as an exhortation to diligently practice.
Chapter Twenty-one: An Exhortation on the Method of Mutual Support Between Good and Evil.

Commentary: This chapter on Mutual Support follows the preceding section because, while the stillness and composure of body and mind belong to one’s own cultivation, the mutual necessity of sentient beings and Buddhas requires that one practice the salvation of others;
thus this position is established to follow the previous chapter, for ordinary people and sages differ.

It is said that good and evil serve as mutual resources for one another; this is called "mutual reliance" (*xiāngzī*). Emperor Xuanzong’s commentary on the *Laozi* explains it as "taking as a resource.
Now, goodness is the teacher of all evils, while evil is the resource for the myriad goods. As the Sutra says: "Sentient beings are able..."
The Buddhas deliver sentient beings, and those Buddhas in turn deliver other sentient beings. Why is this? Because all Buddhas attain the path of Buddhahood precisely because of sentient beings.
As a sutra says: "Lotuses do not grow on high plateaus or dry land; they are born only from within the mud.
Furthermore, all sentient beings attain liberation precisely because of the Buddhas.
The term "the good person" (*śālin*) refers to a human being. As Laozi said: "The good person is the teacher of the not-good person;

the not-good person is the material for the good person. I am merely borrowing that expression here. Regarding the phrase "all [beings] below," it serves as proof for the meaning of sentient beings attaining Buddhahood:
because a Bodhisattva achieves Buddhahood by taking sentient beings as both cause and condition. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Below this... (which follows).
In the "Buddha-Dharma" chapter of that *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, it says: Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, "What is the lineage of the Tathāgata?

Mañjuśrī replied, "If one perceives the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and enters the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), [one cannot again enter the lineage]. (Master Kumārajīva’s commentary states:

From the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*) up to the Arhat, and from the non-arising [wisdom] up to the Buddha—all these are called the stage of certainty. To say "entering by means of the unconditioned" refers to entering the stage of certainty through the perception of signs, and thus taking realization as an object. One cannot again...
The arousal of the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is like this:

just as lotus flowers do not grow on high plateaus or dry land, but rather grow in low-lying, damp mud, so too those who perceive unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and enter the stage of correctness can never again give rise to the Buddha-dharma;
it is only within the mire of afflictions (*kleśa*) that sentient beings can give rise to the Buddha.

[The passage from] the *Dharmakarṇa-sūtra* [states]: "In that sūtra, the fact that flowers do not grow on high ground is a metaphor for the Śrāvakas of the Two Vehicles being unable to give rise to the aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way;
whereas the fact that flowers grow in the mud is a metaphor for sentient beings being able to give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
Therefore, Mahākāśyapa said: 'The host of afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes the seed of the Tathāgata; we, however, are no longer capable of this.'"

Even those who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution are still able to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and be born within the Buddha-dharma; yet we are now forever unable to do so, being like men whose sense organs are destroyed.
This further illustrates the meaning of all Buddhas of inferior light saving sentient beings.

Regarding those called "evil ones," this refers to those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*), violate the four or eight grave prohibitions, slander the noble sages, destroy the wheel of the True Dharma, or are icchantikas.
The Bodhisattva regards such persons as fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Why is this? Because of his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) which is of the same essence [as theirs].
For the sake of beings in the three miserable realms and the four destinies, he undergoes on their behalf sufferings such as having his body shattered, and he draws them forth with gentle speech.

He guides and instructs them to repent, using a compassionate heart to deliver and rescue them so that they may attain happiness. He extensively expounds the ambrosial Dharma, preaching the subtle and wondrous teachings to destroy their evil karma.
With virtuous words he entices and shows them the way, leading them to believe in the ten wholesome paths and be reborn in the realms of humans and devas.

Furthermore, he exhorts them to dedicate these merits toward unexcelled Bodhi. By virtue of this merit, the path of the Bodhisattva is accomplished; thus, even those called sentient beings are able to cross over.

"Buddha. "All evils" refers back to the preceding text. The five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an *arhat*, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha that obstructs the Wheel of Dharma.

The ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) consist of three of the body, four of the speech, and three of the mind. The four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) are: sexual misconduct, stealing, [lying, and intoxicating liquor].

"Killing" refers to falsehood. The eight grave offenses for *bhikṣuṇīs* consist of the eight *pārājikas*; the first four are the same as those for *bhikṣus*, with the addition of [the offenses of] touching, the eighth, concealing, and following [a transgression].

"The seven worthies and sages" refers to the three worthies and the four sages, totaling ten sages. "Destroying the wheel of the True Dharma" is one of the five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).

The *Mātṛkā* states: "To abandon the Eightfold Noble Path and study other paths is the destruction of the wheel. The Commentary on the Precepts (*Jieshu*) says: [This refers to the breaking of the precepts.]
The Wheel of the Dharma (*dharmacakra*) is of two kinds. First, regarding its practice by the practitioner, it is without fault and is likened to a worldly wheel:

right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the hub of morality; right view and right thought constitute the spokes of wisdom; and right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the rim of meditative stabilization.
Expedient means and right effort serve as the person who turns the wheel. If one practices in reliance upon this, one will emerge from the path of birth and death.

Therefore, it is called "conduct" (*caryā*). Second, regarding the teaching: by means of the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma, the transformation reaches the three thousandfold world system, encompassing both monastics and laypeople.
Devadatta proclaimed that the five dharmas were correct and the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) were incorrect;

even the celestial and terrestrial deities proclaimed throughout the three thousandfold world system that the practice of meditation and recitation was no longer to be performed. This is what is meant by being a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). By means of this...
Because the Bodhisattva plants the seeds of the hundredfold adornments upon sentient beings as described above, they are designated as "fields.
Why is this? It is because the Bodhisattva does not disdain their evil but comes to deliver them;

this is due to the fact that their Dharma-body is of one essence and because of the vastness of their compassionate heart. Furthermore, among the four modes of existence, humans and devas possess the capacity for joy.
This partial enumeration of the other four directions merely serves to manifest the arduous efforts of the Bodhisattvas. "Ambrosia" (*amṛta*) is a metaphor for the Dharma-gate;
as the Sūtra says, "opening the gate of ambrosia.

Furthermore, the true nature within one's own body is manifested through human effort; if there were no power of faith, hearing, reflection, and cultivation, [the realization of] all Buddhas and Bodhi...
Although the Bodhisattva possesses compassion, he can do nothing about it.

As for the true nature within the body, it is because all sentient beings inherently possess the one true Buddha-nature. Although this nature is inherently present, it must rely on a person to manifest;
and in manifesting it, there is a method that necessarily relies upon the power of faith as well as the three types of wisdom.

Because faith is the foremost, it is listed first. Confucianism says, "If the people lack faith, they cannot stand. If this were now lacking, the sages and worthies would have no means to transmit their teachings;

thus it is said, "there is nothing that can be done about it. The *Śāsanānuśāsana Sūtra* (The Teaching Left Behind) says, "To guide others toward the path of goodness, if they hear it and do not practice it, the fault does not lie with the guide. Some say that the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Question: Why is it that many [beings] cannot be transformed? Answer: Because the karma of sentient beings is heavy and their delusions are deep, the conditions for goodness are consequently meager;
it is not that the Buddha lacks skillful means. The Great Master once said: "Thus, it is not that the Sage is unable to transform them, but rather that these individuals cannot be transformed.
Therefore, he stands with hands folded, waiting for the opportune moment when their capacity has matured—just as a father [waits for his] infant who is creating evil."
That which your mother did not teach you was not because your parents did not understand how to instruct well; rather, it was simply that an infant cannot be taught.
Therefore, I admonish you: toward all sinful and contemptible beings, you should only give rise to compassion and must not revile them or conceive thoughts of inferiority.
Furthermore, when you see those of superior conduct who are pure and virtuous, you should not treat them with partiality by inviting them alone for offerings.

Why is this? Because good and evil are of one suchness, both being empty by nature; thus, one regards the two views of beauty and ugliness with equanimity, constantly contemplates emptiness and stillness, enters the three gates of liberation, and perceives all classes of sentient beings as like illusions and transformations.
To be unattached to any marks is called the pure mind.
"Deserving of contempt" (*kějiàn*) means "deserving of loathing. Even toward those who are contemptible, one must give rise to a mind of compassion and a desire to rescue and aid them;
they must not be reviled. Does the *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites) not say: "Do not fail to show respect"?

Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states that giving to the lowliest beggar in the city is equal to giving to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha. And the *Sadāparibhūta* says: "I do not dare to treat you with contempt."
"May you all become Buddhas"—this also shows the command to abandon the mind that grasps at signs.
As the Sūtra says: "One should neither mention names nor praise their excellence. Is this not because biased conduct is heavy with faults? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Self-praise and praising others, self-deprecation and deprecating others—these four things are not practiced by the wise. This also refers to not making special invitations or bypassing the order of the monastic assembly.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, it is stated that although one may separately invite five hundred arhats, this still does not constitute inviting the "field of merit" that is the Saṃgha.
Conversely, if one can invite even a single semblance of an extremely wicked bhikṣu from within the Saṃgha, one obtains immeasurable fruit and increases one's merit.

As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains, this is like drinking the water of the ocean, which is to drink all its rivers at once; so too is the invitation of monks according to their order of seniority. This is the case here as well.

This, then, is to suppress the mind of acceptance and rejection and to practice the wisdom of equality. Why? Because it promotes the excellence of being humble toward those below. This is explained as follows:
from the Buddhas above down to sentient beings below, all are one suchness (tathatā) without duality. As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"All are one suchness without duality. Furthermore, Vimalakīrti says: "All sentient beings are suchness; all..."
The Dharma is suchness; the multitude of worthy sages is suchness; even unto Maitreya, it is suchness. Furthermore, the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says:
"Do not revere those who maintain the precepts, nor loathe those who violate them; do not value long-standing practice, nor slight a beginner. Why is this? Because all are awakened.
It is like the light of the eyes, which clearly perceives objects before it; that light is perfect and complete."

There is neither hatred nor love. Why? Because the essence of light is non-dual. "The nature is equally inferior" means that the two natures of good and evil are fundamentally empty from the beginning.
Once this principle is realized, there is no beauty to rejoice in and no ugliness to loathe;

thus it is said that the two views are equal. Regarding "Constantly contemplate," although it is said that the two views are equal, one should contemplate within equality that which is without equality.
When one enters the three samādhis, all marks vanish; only then does one accord with the Way of the pure mind.
The verse says:
If you wish to attain the bliss of liberation, Keep yourself distant and always be close to others; Practice compassion to uproot their suffering.

Having crossed the river of birth and death myself, If one hears of "I" or "the other," This is precisely the demon of discrimination—the view of a self and a life-span— Which the worthy and holy ones alike revile and condemn. The Dharma-realm is of one suchness;
truth and falsehood are like water and its waves. The wave is nothing but water; The water is nothing but the wave.
"Desiring to obtain" refers to the bliss of *nirvāṇa* within the fruits [of practice]. "Distant" refers to the Bodhisattva who does not begrudge body or life;

having become "distant," they constantly exercise compassion to save sentient beings, and thus it is called "intimate. "Other practices" below demonstrate the practice of intimacy with others, which serves as a counter-explanation for the second phrase.
From here on, when one performs altruistic acts through causal practice, the merit is conversely attributed to oneself. This is...
Regarding the meaning of "liberation" in the preceding sentence, it was previously stated that sentient beings are able to deliver the Buddha; this is precisely that meaning.

If one hears the subsequent refutation of attachment and instead becomes attached to hearing it, or if one calculates and clings to "self" and "other," then false discrimination will arise, which again belongs to the work of Māra.
This pertains to the first of the sixteen views, namely the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Therefore, the text subsequently raises the assembly once more.
The "being born" (*jīva*) and the "life-principle" (*jīvaka*) are the second and third of the sixteen types of views.

To speak of a "sentient being" (*sattva*) refers to the false conceptualization of a self within the combination of phenomena such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*); thus it is called the view of a sentient being.

The "view of a life-principle" (*jīvadrṣṭi*) refers to the false conceptualization of a self within these phenomena of name-and-form, aggregates, bases, and elements that experiences [the fruits of] karma.
Because the karmic fruits and lifespans vary in length, they are termed "those who possess a lifespan. The Noble Ones below [the stage of faith] use the Tathāgata to reprove this;

it is known that this correctly destroys the stream of false conceptualizations. Fearing that because of these inversions, all afflictions will arise in full and one will fall into the cycle of birth and death within the *dharmadhātu*, the following passage demonstrates the meaning of the same essence (*tongti*). The *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is the True Suchness of the mind is..."
This is the single Dharma-realm; it is also said that the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body.

Regarding the analogy of water and waves: water represents the True, and waves represent the delusive. If one is deluded regarding the True and gives rise to the delusive, then the entire water is waves.

If one ceases the delusive and returns to the True, then the entire waves return to the water. Water does not depart from the waves, and waves do not depart from the water; their substance is non-dual.
The nature is serene, a single entity without duality; how could there be the two aspects of self and other?
If one can realize this, then the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-spanner are all unobtainable; how then could one give rise to views regarding them?
There are many paths to the gate of goodness, but compassion is the most urgent. For this reason, Sadāprarudita was known in the world as "Ever-Weeping";
out of pity for sentient beings, he abandoned his own joy and embraced sorrowful anxiety. Protecting life is the cause for attaining Buddhahood;
harming life makes the path to Buddhahood arduous. One should give away one's wealth to those in poverty and distress.
Dividing one's food and reducing one's own portions—if one can cultivate even a single moment of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it cannot be matched by sixteen parts of other meritorious gates.
This explains the gift of Dharma; "gate" (*mukha*) has the meaning of "passage," as there are many paths.
Regarding loving-kindness and compassion: because loving-kindness can bestow happiness and compassion can extract suffering, the Bodhisattva initiates their practice by means of these.
It is called "urgent" because it was done previously. *Sadāprarudita* is fully transcribed as *Sadāprarudita*, which means "Constantly Weeping.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that when this Bodhisattva sought Prajñā, he did not spare his own body or life;
furthermore, mindful of his poverty and having nothing with which to make offerings to the Prajñā or the Dharma-preacher, he [encountered] the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

He then cried out, "I wish to sell myself, but no one will buy me. Distressed and weeping, Śakra, wishing to test him, transformed himself into a brāhmaṇa and said, "I now intend to perform a sacrifice to the gods and require human blood, human marrow, and a human heart.

As [the Bodhisattva] was constantly weeping, he immediately took a sharp knife, pierced his arm, cut the flesh from his thigh (the term *bì* has three pronunciations: tōng, bǐ, and bì; it refers to the hip), broke the bone, and extracted [the marrow].
Even if their very marrow were to come forth from their hearts, they would never retreat or regret;

this proves that the Bodhisattva’s practice of seeking the Dharma for the benefit of others—characterized by giving and compassion—is profound indeed. As clarified at length in volumes three hundred and ninety-eight and three hundred and ninety-nine of that sutra, those who "renounce pleasure" do not abide in the bliss of a Bodhisattva, while those who "conceive sorrow" take pity upon sentient beings.

Regarding "suffering" and "protection": because one protects sentient beings out of compassion, entering the Path becomes easy; this is the cause for attaining Buddhahood. The subsequent phrase is the opposite:
entering the Path is slow and difficult. Regarding "lacking wealth": this explains the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).
If one possesses it, one gives away kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and treasures; if one lacks it, one gives even from the contents of one's own alms bowl. Thus says the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*.
The Sūtra states: "Divide the food into four parts. Of the food obtained through begging, give one part to fellow practitioners of the holy life;
the second part to the poor and lowly beggars; the third part to all ghosts and spirits; and the fourth part for one's own sustenance.
Therefore, it is called 'dividing the food and reducing the grains. This is the practice of cultivating a single compassion."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Suppose a person practices great generosity; this does not equal practicing the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

When one practices the samādhi of loving-kindness, sentient beings receive nothing, yet one spontaneously attains immeasurable merit. Of these sixteen parts, [the former] does not equal even one. The *Śāstra* further states:
"In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, the analogy 'sixteen do not equal one' is constantly used; however, in the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is used as follows:"
It is even beyond the reach of calculation or analogy. In the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish), it is divided into sixteen sections, which state:
"If a donor makes separate invitations for sixteen types of recipients, although they obtain a karmic reward, it is not yet considered much.
What are these sixteen? There are eight classes of bhikṣus and eight classes of bhikṣuṇīs; [inviting them] is not as good as..."
[The main text: "If one casually invites four people from among the Sangha, the merit and blessings obtained will exceed those [of the former case];

they do not even reach one-sixteenth part of this. Furthermore, Xiaoyuan said: "Sixteen is also a numerical category, such as when an object weighing one *jin* consists of sixteen *liang*, and so forth."
*Jìngxīn jièguān fāzhēn chāo*, Scroll Lower Part.
