29. Explanation of the Section on Fields of Merit (*Puṇyakṣetra*). Although the nature of benefiting others is no different whether one is born as a sentient being or a Buddha, when categorized by their respective stages and the realization of truth, there is a distinct difference between ordinary beings and sages.
Therefore, this section is established following the preceding one. It is said that because the arising of volition differs, the resulting wisdom is distinguished;

because the production of merit varies, they are designated as "fields" (*kṣetra*) of unequal measure. These are compared in sequence as follows: [The text continues with a comparative analysis of the relative merit derived from offerings made to various fields of merit.]
Regarding the Buddha’s two feet:

having already aroused the great resolve to cultivate the benefit of oneself and others while simultaneously contemplating the Buddha-nature—this constitutes the characteristic of the cause; next, one must contemplate the fruit, which is the Buddha’s wisdom.
Having already arisen, it reaches the characteristics of the cause and connects with the preceding three sections; subsequently, what arises below follows from this.
The Sūtra says: "The wisdom of all sentient beings filling a great trichiliocosm does not equal the wisdom of a single *srotāpanna*;

the wisdom of the *srotāpannas* of a world-system does not equal the wisdom of a single *sakṛdāgāmin*; the wisdom of the *sakṛdāgāmins* of a world-system does not equal the wisdom of a single *anāgāmin*..."

The wisdom of the *anāgāmins* in the world of contained wisdom does not equal one-sixteenth of the wisdom of an *arhat*; the wisdom of an *arhat* does not equal one-sixteenth of the wisdom of a *pratyekabuddha*.
The wisdom of *pratyekabuddhas* filling the worlds of the ten directions does not equal one-sixteenth of the wisdom of a bodhisattva of the lineage (*gotrabhū*).

Thus, by these successive stages, it does not equal one-sixteenth of the wisdom of a bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*). The wisdom of bodhisattvas of the tenth stage filling [the worlds] does not equal that of a Tathāgata.
The wisdom of a single thought-moment is such that even the great ocean of the World-Honored One’s wisdom and all the great beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
though they deliberate together, cannot know the matter of where one will step next. Therefore, you should with single-minded diligence seek the wisdom of the Buddha.
The "Great Trichiliocosm" (Mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu) is the sphere of Śākyamuni’s single transformation. The *Svayaṃpratijñā-samādhi-sūtra* states:
"The Sahā world—'Sahā' being the Chinese translation for 'Endurance World,' while its correct Sanskrit pronunciation is 'Sokha'—is where the Buddha is named Śākyamuni.

This refers to the fact that sentient beings throughout the entire Great Trichiliocosm, including those among humans and the internal and external ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), must reach the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) before they can break through the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*).
In the subsequent verse section, this refers to those who follow through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) within the world—namely, individuals of dull faculties on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
According to the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, the Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Sarvashura:

"If the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with sesame seeds, and if one were to take that quantity [of seeds] as the number of Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*), and if there were a person..."
Since this is so, a wheel-turning monarch is not equal to giving a single *srotāpanna*;

for the *srotāpanna* excels because he has already severed the eighty-eight latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*). He excels the *sakṛdāgāmin* because he has exhausted the six grades of the cultivated delusions (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm.
He excels the *anāgāmin* because he has exhausted the nine grades of the cultivated delusions of the desire realm. He excels the *arhat*... [text truncated]
The Arhat excels [the Pratyekabuddha] because he has completely severed both the views and the afflictions (*kleśa*) within the three realms;
he excels the Bodhisattva of the lineage (*gotra*) because he has already invaded the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*); that is, the stage of the three worthies prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

He excels the ten stages—from the initial Stage of Joy (*pramuditā*) to the final Stage of Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā*)—because he has entered the Mahāyāna lineage. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "He achieves unsurpassed self-benefit."

Because one attains the first stage of the noble ones for the benefit of others and gives rise to great joy; because it is purified of the stains of afflictions that can give rise to errors, such as transgressing the precepts, it is called the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*);
because phenomena appear clearly through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, it is called the Luminous Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*);
and because the fire of wisdom can completely burn the fuel of the afflictions without forgetting them... [it is called the Blazing Wisdom Stage].

Therefore, it is called the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). Because one attains supramundane wisdom and skillful means capable of delivering those who are difficult to deliver, it is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
Because the Great Wisdom of the Prajñāpāramitā manifests before one, it is called the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Because one has well-cultivated the practice of signlessness (*animitta*) and brought its application to completion, thereby being able to transcend the mundane paths of both worldly beings and the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is therefore [called the Ground of Far-Going].
Because the stage of Far-reaching (Dūraṃgamā) is characterized by the ripening of the fruit and the uninterrupted state of signlessness, it is called the Immovable Stage (Acalā).

Because it achieves the practice of benefiting others through unimpeded power in preaching the Dharma, it is called the Good Intelligence Stage (Sādhumatī). Because it possesses mastery over the great Dharmakāya, it is called the Cloud of Dharma Stage (Dharmameghā).
According to this, these ten stages serve as the antidotes to ten types of obscurations; their excellence and breadth are as described [in the scriptures].
Regarding that treatise, Nāgārjuna states that a Tathāgata is so called because he has come by means of the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment;
because all obstacles have been exhausted and his task is complete; and because his wisdom is clear and lucid regarding all objects of knowledge.

Thus, since the wisdom of the Buddha alone is supreme, it is the most excellent. As for the matter of "lifting the foot," this refers to the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata, not that of a Bodhisattva.
Because it is the object of knowledge for the Buddhas and others, the sixty-first volume of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the verses spoken by the Bodhisattva Dharmamati-jvālā-rāja, states:
"The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, along with their great disciples, the Śrāvakas, are all unable to know the Buddha’s lifting and setting down of his feet;

Regarding the matter of lifting and lowering the feet, the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, upper fascicle, states: "The matter of lifting and lowering the feet is something that those on the lower stages cannot perceive.

Furthermore, if one were to offer food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in a single world-system, it would not equal [the merit of]... [the aforementioned].
The merit of giving to those who have not yet attained the stage of Srotāpanna does not equal that of giving to a single Srotāpanna;

this continues through the successive stages until it does not equal that of giving to a single Pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, it is not as good as making offerings to a single Bodhisattva of the same lineage (ekajātīya), nor does it equal the merit of offering to a noble being (ārya) on the first bhūmi, nor the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth bhūmi.

The merit of giving to all these [beings of] the three stages of worthiness and ten stages of holiness for the duration of an entire kalpa does not equal the karmic fruit of offering a single meal to a Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses great wisdom; thus he can digest the offerings and reverences of gods and humans.
Since his wisdom is vast, he can digest many offerings. One who lacks even a single instance of such wisdom cannot digest even water, leaves, or earth.
How much more so for human food?
It does not equal the merit of making offerings to the Tathāgata, because when the three types of awakening are perfected, the resulting merit is greatest.

As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom) states: "An old woman gave the Buddha some foul-smelling dregs and attained the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, King Aśoka, while still a youth...
When as a child he offered earth to the Buddha, King Yaṃvūdvīpa attained the Way last of all; how much more so when one offers the four requisites of a hundred flavors to the Buddha?
This is identical to the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*, though there are slight differences in the sequence;
therefore, that text says: "The Buddha said: To feed a hundred evil people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person; to feed a thousand virtuous people is not as good as..."
Feeding one who observes the five precepts is ten thousand times superior to feeding those who observe the five precepts;
feeding one *srotāpanna* is superior to feeding a million *srotāpannas*; feeding one *sakṛdāgāmin* is superior to feeding ten million *sakṛdāgāmins*;
feeding one *anāgāmin* is superior to feeding a hundred million *anāgāmins*; and feeding one *arhat* is superior to feeding a billion *arhats*.
A hundred million arhats are not equal to feeding one pratyekabuddha; feeding ten trillion pratyekabuddhas is not equal to feeding one Buddha of the three periods of time;
feeding a thousand million billion Buddhas of the three periods of time is not equal to feeding one who is without thought, without dwelling, without cultivation, and without realization.
Master Yuan’s commentary states: this refers to the generation of the great mind (bodhicitta).

The Bodhisattva’s perfect understanding is vast and open, pervasive and unimpeded. There is no wisdom that can conceive it, no principle upon which it dwells, no cause to be cultivated, and no fruit to be realized.
Since both subject and object, cause and effect, are entirely non-apprehendable, the attainment of the Bodhisattva’s wondrous fruit is spontaneously accomplished.
If one were to offer food to such a person, why would their merit surpass that of all Buddhas?
Answer: The Buddhas have already realized [enlightenment] and no longer rely on external conditions; however, the bodies of those at the initial stage of the path still depend on sustenance.

If their food and drink are sufficient, they can proceed toward the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*); if they suffer from hunger and thirst, it will hinder their cultivation of the correct contemplation (*samyak-darśana*).

Therefore, by giving them superior food, one effectively makes offerings to the Buddhas. In the present text, the mention of "the Buddhas" refers to the ultimate attainment of the fruit, while "water and vegetables" refers to the basic requisites for practice.
If even the products of the earth, which require no human labor to produce, cannot be consumed [without offense], how much less so fine garments and delicacies?

The Buddha said: "If there are those who are neither śramaṇas nor practitioners of the brahma-faring, yet claim to be śramaṇas and practitioners of the brahma-faring, they would have no place on this great earth even to spit or discharge phlegm, let alone to lift their feet, set them down, come and go, or bend and stretch their limbs. Why is this?"
"In the past, great kings bestowed this great earth as a gift upon those who maintained the precepts and possessed virtue;
however, one who lacks the knowledge of cessation cannot accept it.

You should understand the fundamental intent of this admonition: cultivate pure precepts so that they are not deficient or transgressed, for it is through the purity of the precepts [that such gifts may be received]."

It is easy to attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), through which the concentrated mind becomes pure, giving rise to wisdom and the fulfillment of merit, thereby perfecting the fivefold Dharma-body and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
As stated in Vasubandhu’s *Śikṣāsamuccaya-śāstra*: "Both mundane and supramundane meditative concentrations arise in dependence upon the precepts."
It is said that the manifestation of the merits of liberation, both with form and without form, all arise from this;
thus, "omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the wisdom realized by the Buddhas.
Now, the power of the Buddhas' wisdom shall be briefly explained once more.
In a single instant, they know the number of drops from a fine rain falling simultaneously throughout the worlds of the ten directions over many years and months;

they know the total measure in *hu* and *dou* of all the rivers and seas of the ten directions; they universally know the weight in *jin* and *liang* of the Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Sumeru, and the great earth;
and they skillfully know the number of atoms within the lands of the Dharma-realm, or the mental activities of sentient beings pervading the entire realm of empty space.

Each and every sentient being knows that he will become a Buddha in such-and-such an eon; he can place the mountains, seas, heavens, earth, suns, and moons of the ten directions within the palm of his hand and travel through the worlds, yet Śakra and Brahmā do not perceive his coming or going. He can inhale the waters and fires of the ten directions into his mouth;
the water does not extinguish him, and the fire does not harm his mouth. If one were to describe this in full detail, it would be inexhaustible.

The Cakravāḍa and Sudarśana mountains are each twenty-three thousand four hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth, with a circumference of three hundred seventy thousand three hundred and fifty *yojanas*. Sumeru is correctly called Sumeru;

it is translated as "Wondrously High" (*Miaogao*), so named because it is composed of the four precious substances—namely, gold on the eastern face, lapis lazuli on the southern, silver on the western, and crystal on the northern—and because it rises seven [times higher than its base].

The name [of the mountain] is renowned as being beyond the Golden Mountain; the *Abhidharmakośa* states that it emerges eighty thousand *yojanas* above the water and likewise enters the water to the same depth.
Each terrace atop the Golden Wheel is like what is described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
'In the future, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named the Tathāgata Padmaprabha; the land shall be named Vimalā. Furthermore, he said:
Pūrṇa said, "After immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this land,

Such supernormal powers arise from the five contemplations for cessation (pañca-viṣkambhanā), arise from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ), arise from the four immeasurables (catvāry-apramāṇāni), arise from the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitāḥ), and arise from the ten stages of the Mahāyāna (daśa-bhūmayaḥ). These are called the power of wisdom and the power of supernormal faculties of all Buddhas;
they arise from severing wealth and sensual desire through the five contemplations for cessation.
The eight characters from "From the severing of wealth and form" (*cāi-se*) onward appear to be a repetition, or perhaps they may be understood as a restatement.

From the time the causal arousal [of the mind] occurred, the successive stages of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have led up to the present stage of Buddhahood; this is precisely the manner in which the characteristics of the beginning and end of this admonition are explained.

Since the beginning of its arising, it proceeds from the introduction and the fundamental tenets; first, the admonitions regarding wealth and women, followed by the five cessations (*pañca-vyupaśama*), all belong to the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*).
Reaching the stage of Buddhahood is the fruition (*phala*); therefore, this is called "explaining the characteristics from beginning to end."
The distinct stages of the Bodhisattva’s successive practices are as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This is extensively elucidated in such sections as the "Ten Grounds" (*Daśabhūmika*) chapter of that very scripture.
You should plant the seeds of compassion within the field of sentient beings, and place the seeds of reverence within the field of the Three Jewels.

When the sprouts of merit and wisdom arise, they become the Bodhi-tree that provides shade for the entire Dharma-realm; throughout the ten directions, flowers bloom and the unsurpassed fruit is realized.
You should plant the seeds of various sutras; although some speak of three fields of merit, here we speak of only two.

Briefly stated, regarding the field of gratitude—specifically toward one's parents and teachers—one must plant the seeds of filial piety. For the time being, the assignments are as follows; this must be so.
When seeds are mutually pervasive, it is truly excellent; for when parents are in the midst of illness and suffering, how could one lack a heart of compassion?

If one nurtures them yet lacks reverence, one is no different from a dog or a horse—how could such a person lack a heart of respect? When the Buddha-Dharma is about to perish, how could one lack a heart of compassion?

To be filial toward one's teachers and the Triple Gem is to possess a heart of filial piety; to look upon the lowliest beggar in the city as equal to the Invincible One (Duṣprasaha) [is likewise required].
Are the Tathāgatas and others not worthy of our veneration? Have they not all been our parents in the past, such that we would lack filial piety toward them?

For now, however, we speak in terms of those who are preeminent; therefore, we address them specifically. Furthermore, the *Śīla-sūtra* states that there are eight fields of merit: first, the Buddha; second, holy persons;
third, the upādhyāya; fourth, the ācārya; fifth, the Saṃgha; sixth, the father; seventh, the mother; and eighth, the sick person.

From the initial aspiration for the Way until its ultimate consummation, all intervening functional activities are termed "obstructions to knowledge. Upon reaching the stage of a Tathāgata, these two obstructions are forever exhausted.
Looking back upon saṃsāra, it is seen as being like an illusion or a dream, fundamentally lacking reality and deceiving only the deluded;
because only the Buddha possesses correct awakening, he is called the "Omniscient One" (Sarvajña).
All are termed "obstructions to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); if one stagnates in their functional application, this constitutes an obstruction within the realm of wisdom.

There are two obstructions: first, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and second, the obstruction to the knowable. It is not that the knowable itself is the obstruction; rather, because this obstruction obstructs the knowable, it is called the "obstruction to the knowable.
Looking back from this toward the ultimate fruit below, and looking back from this toward the cycle of birth and death previously experienced:
All transformations are like illusions and dreams.

Because it is unfathomable, it is like the ocean of the world.
The verse says:

The stages of the pratyekabuddhas; the stages of those on the ten bhūmis; the distinctions of wisdom—these do not equal the body of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the character "xíng" (行) in "xíngxízhě" (信行者), it is an error inherited from the preceding rhyme and should be "zhì" (智); this refers to the two [types of practitioners] within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

As for riding in a carriage, since the time of the Han dynasty, the Son of Heaven has used it; a sedan chair without wheels is called a *yu*.

Regarding the two lines [of the verse] beginning with "having not yet eaten," the Wise One rebuked them as follows: as the *I Ching* says, "To carry a burden and yet ride in a carriage leads to the capping of one's head";

and as Confucius said, "To carry a burden and yet ride in a carriage is also shameful. For those who study the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), if they do not enter through the gradual stages, then...

Because they lack cultivation regarding these matters, the Tathāgata is not pleased. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The bhikṣus neglected the study of the Vinaya and instead recited the Sūtras and Abhidharma.
The World-Honored One rebuked them in various ways, concluding that it is only because the Vinaya exists that the Dharma remains in the world.
Regarding the phrase "the seal of the ruler" (*guojun yin*), E Shao stated: "‘Er’ means to believe. (From the *Gujin yuelu*).

Seals and insignia are collectively termed *yin* (seals), transmitted by both the noble and the humble alike. As for the nomenclature established under the Qin dynasty, it was not universally applied;

yet when the Qin obtained the Jade of He, one tradition says it was called "Lanyou," and from that jade a seal was fashioned. Its inscription read: "Mandated by Heaven, may his life be long and ever-prosperous.
The Chancellor, Li Si, engraved this in seal script (*zhuanshu*). This was indeed a portent of national auspiciousness—how could it be considered vulgar?
That which my husband holds, I now illustrate by means of the seal: the True Dharma is empty, while the base man is one who has not studied the precepts.

This present admonition is devoid of ornate artifice; out of deep compassion for you, it points directly to the facts with concise restraint. Furthermore, I regret that you have presumptuously allowed yourself to be soiled [by worldly concerns].

Because the Master was initially ignorant regarding instruction, he sent forth words that pierce the heart with bitterness, as if speaking face-to-face, to bring your practice of the Way to completion.
Now that you have realized this for yourself, you should in turn teach your fellow students and other wise ones. I am extremely frail and my past merits do not provide security;
should I not see you, these are my final instructions. They are not merely earnest words, but a sincere exhortation to purify your mind.

"One whose essence is devoid of flowery merit" means that their speech does not employ flowery, ornate, or clever rhetoric. Yang Xiong said, "Carving insects and engraving seals—these are not the pursuits of a noble man.
Furthermore, the use of the term "Great Master" below [the title] expresses humility. "Mao-wang" (冒罔) means to venture forth or to surpass.

As for "turning the teaching to one's fellow students," this reflects the Sage’s intent: he did not limit his care to his own son alone, but commanded that the instruction be passed on and guided; thus, they are likewise Bodhisattvas.
Regarding this great practice, those with remaining wisdom can believe and accept it through their intelligence; however, if one is a *icchantika* or a fool, they will not receive it.
The Confucian says: "O Master, this youth is difficult to speak with. The Superior also said: "Why trouble yourself to see such a person?
This refers to one who has not secured peace in their past lives—one who speaks of momentary arising and ceasing while claiming to have faith.
"One's lodging cannot be guaranteed" means that one leaves behind only virtuous words as a final testament regarding one's conduct.

When it says "the intent is not earnest," does this mean the words themselves are not earnest? Furthermore, these are terms used for concise summaries; what was previously called a "brief narration" refers to this very point.
Nevertheless, although the text contains many meanings, its primary purpose is to cause one to follow the path as cautioned above.
One returns to the pure mind. Now, since one perceives the moon by following the finger and enters the Way through words, this admonition for contemplation must not be absent for even a single day.
I have often lamented that while the essential points of this literature for awakening and guidance are supreme, those who transmit and chant them are increasingly few;
this is merely a failure to repay the kindness of the former sages. Thus, as I address the incense burner with a sigh of regret, I release my words, unaware of how they flow forth.

I, Ying, value self-reflection above all else and dare not neglect others; I hope to rely on this cause to cultivate great conduct, to uproot all beings from the nine realms of existence, and to bring them close to the Sages throughout the ten directions.
May they realize the source of their own minds and reach the ultimate state of Buddhahood.

It is my earnest wish that all who see or hear of this shall universally honor the pure mind, and that as they take each step upon the path, they shall all head toward the Precious Abode. With a mere snap of the fingers— [The text concludes here.]
With palms joined, may all attain the fruit of Buddhahood; throughout all future births, may my vow never decay. As I reach the end of this writing, I am moved by the sacred power and shed tears.
May those who read this later understand my resolve.
*Jìngxīn jièguān fāzhēn chāo*, Scroll Lower, End (Concluded).
Transmitted by the Vinaya-preaching monk Dàojiàn of the Pútí Jiàoyuàn in Lín'ān Prefecture, who, using his own robes, bowl, and funds,
engraved this one volume of three fascicles along with its ritual manual for perpetual and widespread circulation, so that the *Vinaya* may flourish.

Jiuzhu (Long-Abiding) further records this to repay the four debts of gratitude and to provide merit for the three realms of existence. Written on the Double Ninth Festival in the third year of the Jiading era.
